speechtext: I have the honour to inform the House that a bust of Lord Durham has been presented to the Dominion of Canada by Mr. John St. Loe Strachey, of London, England, and has been received in Ottawa to-day. It will be installed somewhere in the House of Commons this afternoon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BUST PRESENTED TO CANADA BY MR. STRACHEY
speechtext: In connection with the announcement which Your Honour has just made, I am sure I voice the feeling of hon. members of this House when I say that we all deeply appreciate the generous gift which has been made by Mr. Strachey and should be glad if Your Honour would express to him the thanks of this House.

Mr. A. TV. NEILL (Comox-Alberni): Before the orders of the day are called I desire to direct the attention of the government to a newspaper report and to ask a couple of simple questions in connection therewith. The report to which I have reference appears in the Montreal Gazette of Saturday last. Special from the Gazette's resident staff correspondent by wireless registered in accordance with Copyright Act.
I shall not read the whole of it but the following three or four lines are decidedly of interest:
Meighen's name curiously enough was among those* recently mentioned in two London newspapers as a likely successor of Lord Byng.
I want to ask two questions:	Is the

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:

On the Orders of the Day:
Mr. HARRY J. BARBER (Fraser Valley): I desire to ask the Minister of Justice a question based upon the following article which appears in the Vancouver Daily Province of April 21:
Sumas landowners have forwarded a petition to Ottawa asking that certain provincial legislation be disallowed. The act to which they object is one passed at the last session of the legislature which validates all actions of the dyking commissioners and stipulates that the assessment roll "shall not be quashed or set aside or the validity thereof otherwise questioned on any ground whatsoever."
Numerous property owners affected by the reclamation work are reported to have signed the petition. They attacked the assessment roll last year, asked for the accounting and alleged that the Land Settlement Board, as dyking commissioners, "illegally, negligently, recklessly, wrongfully and without authority and in breach of their duties as commissioners spent *large sums of money in constructing works within the Sumas dyking district."
Their action in petitioning Ottawa goes back to Magna Charta for precedent, it being a principle of the British constitution that any subject may approach the king. Provincial legislation, it is claimed, removed any right of Sumas property owners affected by reclamation works to redress in the courts. It is upon *this that they are asking for the disallowance of the legislation, claiming that the legislation complained of is ultra vires.
I would ask the Minister of Justice if this petition has been received; if so, will he have the correspondence laid on the table, and has he reached any decision in the matter?

CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I ask my hon. friend,
who on this side ever argued that it is bad to have an excess of exports over imports?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have heard that argument advanced on several occasions by hon. gentlemen opposite.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Never.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just wait a
moment. I have heard it argued by my hon. friends opposite that we should not sell our raw materials.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will get to
that later.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Get to it now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly we are
selling raw materials. What nation does not? We are selling our wheat and our flour in the markets of the world. The United States sells her cotton and her oil in the markets of the world; and certainly crude oil is a raw product. So we are doing what every other nation is doing, we are exporting the excess of our raw materials that cannot be manufactured and sold at home; and no one will question the wisdom of that policy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Could the minister tell
us what proportion of our exports is raw material, and what proportion of United States exports is raw material?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It^would not be difficult to find that information.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have it. That would
be very appropriate to give the House now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You can do it at the proper time, but not just now.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In following my
argument, Mr. Speaker, I wish to be very brief. When one hears the statement that Canada is being flooded with foreign goods, it would seem well to consider the trade between Canada and . the various countries of the world, to see how our trade has progressed during the last ten years. In 1914 our imports from Great Britain amounted to $132,070,408; in 1924, they totalled $153,586,690. Our exports in 1914 were $222,322,292 and in 1924, $361,160,802. I do not propose to deal with all the various nations, but I do wish to consider the trade between Canada and the United States. In 1914 we imported from the LTnited States $396,302,138 worth of goods; in 1924, our imports amounted to $601,256,417. In 1914 we exported to the United States goods to the value of $176.948,299; in 1924, our exports amounted to $441,642,909. We have heard a great deal about the unfavourable trade balance with the United States. If hon. gentlemen opposite look at these figures they will see that during the last few years there has been an equalization in that trade. I have given the figures for 1924, and the figures for 1925, if given, would show' an even more favourable condition.
We have heard a great deal regarding our trade with France; hon. members opposite have criticized from time to time the trade treaty entered into by Canada and France. Let us look at trade conditions as they
2840	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)
existed in 1914 between France and Canada, and then consider them in 1924. In 1914 our imports from France amounted to $14,276,535; in 1924 our imports totalled $15,767,851. In 1914 we exported to France goods to the value of $3,632,444, and in 1924 our exports amounted to $18,879,097. In 1914 there was a balance of a million dollars against us, but in 1924 the balance of trade was some $15,000,000 in our favour.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the minister please tell us when the change took place?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is taking place every day. We are selling to France more than ever.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the change been gradual,, or has it come within the last two or three years?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend
will understand that I am taking these two periods, the year before the war and some years after. I am not complicating these statistics with war periods, because I do not think that, would be fair or proper. We are now some seven or eight years away from the war, and we can make a comparison of conditions as they are now with those existing before the war.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the minister give us the figures for the period just before the treaty was negotiated, and for the period immediately afterwards?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That will be
shown later; it has been shown in this House on a number of occasions, and I am not dealing with it to-day.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the minister give us the balance of trade for the year before the treaty went into effect and for the last year, which would be a fair comparison?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think
my hon. friend could have heard me. I stated that I kept the accounting to the year before the war and to 1924, some years following the war. I do not wish to prolong the discussion; I am trying to show that during that ten year period, following a time of great stress during which this country acquired new obligations, we emerged with a favourable trade balance which was not enjoyed in 1914.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Might I ask the minister if it would not be more fair to give the year immediately before the treaty went into effect, and the last year?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think
that is necessary for the purposes of my argument. My hon. friend has discussed the French treaty from time to time, not always on the basis of the treaty; he has placed his own interpretation on it. These figures are chosen for the purposes of this argument, which I hope will be of some benefit to my hon. friends opposite, who from time to time during the last three or four years have made it their business to go up and down this country informing the people that our business was not improving; that conditions were not healthy, and that Canada was on the verge of bankruptcy. I hope to dispel that feeling not only in this House but throughout the country. If the figures I have, which are reliable, are known to the Canadian people, I am satisfied that all sign of despair will disappear and that the optimism with which the budget has been received will be considerably strengthened.
Japan is a country with which we have a considerable trade. In 1914 our imports from Japan amounted to $2,604,216; in 1924 they amounted to $6,298,201. Our exports in 1914 totalled $1,587,467, while in 1924 they amounted to $26,991,860. The same thing applies to China; the trade balance ha3 changed in our favour.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Might I ask a question? What did those exports consist of?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Many articles
made in Canada. Our Canadian manufacturers are entering the Japanese field. Wheat played a very large part in this favourable balance, but our merchants and our cattle producers in western Canada are also shipping their products into the Japanese market with marked success.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of that total, what
proportion is composed of manufactured
goods?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not an
encyclopaedia. The information requested by my hon. friend can be easily secured; if I were to speak to-morrow I would secure that information for him. We do know that during the last ten years our trade with Japan has expanded until now, instead of the unfavourable balance which existed in 1914, we have a very favourable balance as shown by the figures I have just given.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Our exports consisted largely of raw materials.

speechtext: Rot.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is that so, or is it
not?

The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I told my hon. friend, a large amount of wheat has been exported to Japan, which might be called raw material. Possibly it would be advantageous to the Canadian people to make that wheat into flour, but it is no more raw material than is cotton in the United States.

Would my hon. friend

Might I suggest to hon.

CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As I have been quoted, Mr. Speaker, may I rise to a question of privilege? I made no such statement as has been quoted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Nothing could
give me greater pleasure than to hear that statement from my hon. friend. He was generally reported throughout the press in British Columbia as having made a statement of that character, and knowing the gloomy attitude which he takes of things as they exist in Canada to-day, one could very well assume that that statement represented his attitude.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
I rise to a point of order,
Mr. Speaker. The hon. Minister of Public Works is commenting on a statement attributed to me in the public press, which statement I have denied. Now I want to state, Mr. Speaker, that the statement I did make was this-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think I have the floor, Mr. Speaker, and I will retain the floor till I am through. My hon. friend has already spoken in this debate.

speechtext: May I say-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Sit down, please. The
hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard rose to deny the statement attributed to him in the press despatch which the hon. Minister of Public Works was reading. The hon. Minister of Public Works then rose and did accept the hon. member's statement immediately, but he was proceeding to make an explanation when the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard rose again to make another denial. The hon. member has already denied in toto the statement attributed to him in the press, and the hon. Minister of Public Works, as every member of the House must do, has accepted his word.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I state, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not unless it is another
point of order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am just asking a question, Mr. Speaker. May I state, as a matter of privilege, what I did say on that occasion?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, because it would be against the rules.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I have said,
I am delighted to have my hon. friend deny that statement. No one more readily accepts his denial than myself because I could not believe, in fact, I know that the conditions in British Columbia do not warrant that statement. I hold in my hand a statement that was published in the Vancouver Province, a paper not a supporter of this government, but an excellent paper that tries to present and does give to the people of British Columbia in a general way the news of the day. In its issue of April 11, 1926, it says:
to,000,000 building outlay for first quarter, 1926: $7,250,000 locally subscribed for British Columbia Electric loan. British Columbia Electric Bpending $30,000,000 in development. $160,000,000 British Columbia Electric payroll.
If I may be allowed an interjection here, it is with some satisfaction that I note our

present industrial payroll in British Columbia is $160,000,000, because on looking back to the year 1922, I find that the industrial payroll of British Columbia was then $120,000,000. It goes on:
Vancouver regular port of call for 42 steamship
lines. 916 ships entered Vancouver harbour in 1925.
That is an inspiring statement, one that will do much to inspire the people of British Columbia, and I believe that if the people of eastern Canada would take advantage of conditions as they exist to-day and set fairly before the people of Canada those conditions, there would be more optimism and less pessimism than we have to-day, and it would be to the advantage of Canada as a whole.
When the Minister of Finance brought down his budget the other day the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), owing to the illness of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), replied on behalf of the opposition. I think we all admired the ease with which the hon. gentleman spoke, and the manner in which he developed his reply. He accepted the good things in the budget, the reductions in taxation, as being all right. Then he placed on Hansard certain figures, but those figures- whether due to lack of time in preparation or lack of opportunity for verification on his part-will stand examination and should be examined and discussed here. The hon. gentleman caused it to be inferred that this government had by means of the reduction in the British preference placed the woollen industry in a precarious condition in Canada. This is what he said:
In the first year two and a half per cent was taken off the duty on woollen goods. The Laurier-Fielding tariff had served the country, so well, that had kept the mills so busy, was tinkered with in the first year and reduced to 27) per cent. In the following year there was another cut of ten per cent in the British preferential bringing the tariff on woollens down from 27) per cent to 24.8 per cent net, and what was the result? All over Canada woollen mills began to close; men lost their jobs, the exodus started to the United States and woollen men would not invest more money. I say to the Minister of Finance: Look at your imports of woollens for those years. See them gradually rising in this country until last year, according to the government's trade returns of which I have a copy in my hand, we brought in $20,000,000 worth of woollen goods from Great Britain, all of wh:eh we could have made in Canadian mills if the Prime Minister had had resolution and courage enough to stand by the tariff which he helped to make in 1007.
Now, let us look at the woollen industry and see what has happened. In 1921 our total importation of dutiable woollen goods from Great Britain amounted to $45,795,573.
In 1922 we imported $22,895,016 worth; in

The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)
1923, $31,298,216 worth; in 1924, $30,447,895 worth; and in 1925, $30,283,675 worth. Now it may be that the importation of $20,000,000 to which the hon. gentleman referred had reference only to certain woollens. The figures I have given, however, cover the total importations of woollen goods from Great Britain. It will be noted that in 1921, owing to conditions that existed in Canada after the war-I wish to be fair-and before any tariff changes had taken place we imported $45,795,000 worth of woollen goods. In 1925, the importation had dropped to $30,283,000 worth. However, I wish to go on and follow the matter a little further. We have a great woollen industry in Canada known as Penman's Limited. This firm manufactures woollen garments and is a really great organization. We find that in 1921 they manufactured woollen goods to the extent of $4,789,053. In 1925, the amount had risen to $6,431,153. Apparently the Penman's are enjoying to-day a larger amount of business, at least their sales are greater, than in 1921 by almost $2,000,000. Now, if you go back and take the importation of $45,000,000 odd in 1921 as against $30,000,000 odd in 1925 you must go beyond the tariff changes to find the explanation for the diminution. The explanation must be found in some other cause because we find a decline in the sale of woollens in the United States. In that country, which our Conservative friends would lead the people to believe is not only the most highly protected but the most prosperous country in the world, no industry, they say, goes out of business because the government immediately comes to its rescue. Now, what do we find in the United States? In 1923 the average monthly consumption of woollens amounted to 53,467.000 pounds, whereas in 1925 it had dropped to 43,857,000 pounds. What, is the reason for that? It is not because there was not a tariff. We know, every man knows that in his own home to-day, woollen goods are not being used to the extent that they were used years ago:	They are being replaced by goods
that are made from a mixture of wool, cotton, silk, and artificial silk. The result is that to-day the woollen industry, not only in Canada but throughout the world, is obliged to adjust itself to new conditions.
But I should like to deal for a moment with a further statement made by my hon. friend, as follows:
"I am witling to stand by my statement. Cultivators in the days of the Lauriei-Fielding tariff, when the present Prime Minister was a member of the government of that day and supported the tariff in that government, enjoyed a duty of 17i per cent. This government has cut the duty down now to 7J per
cent. No wonder that the trade has been almost abandoned in this country and our farmers are very largely being supplied with goods from the United States."
Now, Mr. Speaker, I contend that that statement does not correctly represent the condition as far as the manufacturer of agricultural implements in this country is concerned. We find that in 1922 the people of Canada imported binders amounting to $319807 in value. In 1925 they imported $216,427 worth. The hon. member for South Wellington did not refer to reapers, but I shall give the figures for that branch of the industry also. In 1922 we imported 6,805 reapers, and in 1925 reapers to the number of 198. In 1922 we bought $36,143 worth of mowers, and in 1925 mowers amounting in value to $27,930. We will now see what the export business by the manufacturers of agricultural implements amounted to in those years. In 1922 we exported $449,013 worth of binders. In 1925 the export amounted to $1,220,000 worth. In 1922, we exported reapers to a total amount of $12,901 worth, and in 1925 the value of the export of reapers was $105,893 worth. Of mowers in 1922 we exported $369,762 worth, and in 1925, a value of $957,695, showing that during that period the agricultural implement men had improved their position in the matter of export and had conserved the home market to a greater extent. Now as to the plow industry which was said to be ruined:	In 1922,
we imported $554,846 worth of plows, and in 1925, plows to the amount of $613,998. In 1922, the export, of plows amounted to $1,465,919 worth, and in 1925 we exported $1,630,908 worth, showing a favourable condition as regards exports and also as regards the home market.
Now let us take the total trade in agricultural implements. The total importations in 1921 amounted to $24,317,190 worth, and the exports to $12,527,000. In 1925 we imported only $6,428,000 worth. We sold $11,342,000 worth. There is no question with regard to the manufacture of agricultural implements. We were told in 1924 the reduction the government then made would destroy that industry. We know that to-day the Massey-Harris stock is selling for more than it was previous to that date. We know that many of the factories in this country are enjoying great prosperity, and we know from the trade returns that the change has not seriously affected the agricultural implement industry.
I have stated that this budget is appreciated by the Canadian people. It is a budget that goes into every home in this country. My

The Budget-Mr. King (Kootenay)
hon. friend the former Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie), complained the other day that the government's budget was two or three years too late. He overlooked the fact that in 1924 this government had a surplus of many millions of dollars, and at that time, brought about by reduction in customs duties and sales taxes, the government contributed some $20,000,000 odd to the relief of the Canadian taxpayer. That should not be overlooked, and when my hon. friend claims that the delay had been too great he did not give consideration to the fact that this government in 1924 did make reductions in taxation amounting to something over $20,000,000 or $25,000,000. A reduction in sales taxes will always be acceptable to the Canadian people, and it is the desire of the government, and I think ot the people of Canada, that we be relieved of that burden as early as possible. It is true that the sales tax is a convenient way of raising revenue. We are. told that this government had increased the sales tax from two and a half to six per cent, but if hon. members will go back to the period of 1923 and 1924, and read Mr. Fielding's statement on the sales tax, they will realize that the sales tax as administered by the late government did not bring revenue, because it was not collectable, and where it was collected it had pyramided itself. It has been found that the amendments made by Mr. Fielding have been effective in securing revenue, and it has been the policy of this government, when conditions permitted in the country, to reduce that tax on these commodities that would first give relief to the people in the homes of this country.
The reduction in postage will certainly not *be criticized. I think the Canadian people are to be congratulated that we are to go back to the day of penny postage, and as the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) said the other day, the Canadian people being the first to introduce penny postage, would come back again to thit period with great gratification and pleasure.
The abolition of the receipt tax will give to the merchant and to the individual who is buying or selling relief from what has been termed a nuisance. It was not a large revenue producer, and the government, as the minister has said, considered it wise to abolish that tax. I am satisfied that the change will be acceptable to the people of Canada. The reduction in income tax has given general satisfaction to those who have been paying the tax.
I have listened for the last week to discussion on the budget as occasion permitted me, and generally speak in =* from the opposite

side of the House the argument has not been greatly against the budget as introduced by the minister. Exception however has been taken to the reduction in the automobile tax and it was on that score that the 4 p.m hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) moved his amendment a few days ago, stating that the government should not have made the reduction in the automobile tax without referring this matter to the tariff board. One would think, after hearing hon. gentlemen opposite, that this was a new thing in the public mind of Canada. I cannot conceive that members who were in the last parliament who heard the debate and witnessed the vote in that parliament could have been deceived as to the minds of the Canadian public representatives in this parliament in the matter of automobile taxation, because last year, when the resolution was introduced by the hon. member for Macleod, (Mr. Coote), we found members from every group in the House supporting the proposed reduction. The government would have been remiss if, after that debate and that vote, they had not given very careful and thorough consideration to the question of reduction of duties on automobiles. It may be convenient for hon. members opposite to say that this question should not have been dealt with by parliament but should have been referred to the tariff commission, but that course would not have satisfied the majority in parliament or the majority of the people of Canada, because conditions had arrived in connection with the manufacture of automobiles that required adjustment. I claim that the government have acted wisely and properly in the matter. It is true that some men will, as the ostrich does, place their heads in the sand so that they will not see what is coming, but any business man engaged in the industry of manufacturing automobiles, after hearing the debate in this House, should have realized that, in the public mind throughout Canada, there was a feeling that the day had arrived when there should be an adjustment in the duties on automobiles. So that we cannot, Mr. Speaker, take too seriously our hon. friends opposite. I have heard only one hon. member-and this my hon. friend from Burrard (Mr. Clark) will not deny-on the Conservative side state in his place that if his party were returned to power he would vote for and see that there was a return to the former duty.

That in the opinion o-f this House, a substantial reduction in the 'import duties on agricultural implements is now due the agriculturists of Canada, and is in just accord with the true ends of a protective tariff.
It is interesting to read the remarks of the right hon. gentleman made at that time, when although he was much younger than he is now he had the same faculty for acute reasoning and getting at his point. His argument on that occasion was that, the agricultural implement industry having pretty well secured the home market in Canada and having ventured into foreign fields, the time had come when there should be substantial reductions in duty. It is rather a remarkable coincidence that the agricultural implement industry at that time enjoyed a duty of 35 per cent, and the leader of the opposition evidently came to the same conclusion then as this government has arrived at in respect of the automobile industry. The reduction then was from 35 to 20 per cent.

were asking for a reduction. To substantiate his case the leader of the opposition quoted Sir George Foster, who at that time was Minister of Finance:
The reduction in agricultural implements from 35 per cent to 20 per cent is one under which it would tax the ingenuity of the manufacturers to keep the field against what is now keen competition especially in the northwest.
Commenting on that quotation he said:
Thus did he postulate that the test by which these duties were to be judged, the guide by which he was to be governed, was such a duty as, ait the narrowest point, would test the ingenuity of the manufacturers to keep the field against foreign competition.

That they believe that our people can compete with less protection than formerly and to prove that it can be pointed out that we are now sending agricultural implements to many portions of the world.

I do not say that a reduction will to any very enoimous extent affect the price; I believe it will materially, and I think it will render some relief to particularly the farmers of the west. It will afford some relief to them and I believe it is the bounden duty of the government to so afford it

I corrected myself. As I said, the leader of the opposition was quoting arguments that had been used by Sir George Foster when he was Minister of Finance, Sir George having pointed out that prior to 1896 there had been a reduction from 35 to 20 per cent. The leader of the opposition in the debate to which I refer enunciated certain guiding principles. He laid down three basic principles: First, that a duty must never be higher than is sufficient at the narrowest point to test the ingenuity of the manufacturers to meet the keenest possible competition. That is good reasoning, and it was advanced by the right hon. gentleman at that time as an argument in favour of his proposed reduction in duties. Secondly, that the duty must be maintained not until the Canadian industry has overtaken the whole consumption, but only until the indus-

He was not suggesting that the industry should saturate the home market before the duty was reduced but that it should only partially cover the market. Thirdly, that the moment the home industry is able to export its products into foreign markets, that moment the duty should be taken off or at least materially decreased.
In view of the foregoing arguments surely we have arrived in Canada at the point where substantial reductions in the duties on automobiles should be made, especially when we know that last year the manufacturers exported from 40 to 42 per cent of their output. I do not think therefore that we need be disturbed by the activity of some motor dealers and manufacturers in this country, who on the day the budget came down closeted themselves in their offices and without notifying their employees had notices prepared and posted on their doors next morning informing the public and employees that their plant had been closed until they could ascertain just what the budget meant. Now that meant no expense to the manufacturers, but the two or three days during which the plant was closed down the employees suffered in the matter of loss of their wages. If the General Motors concern had been dealing with a rising market and were going to charge from $150 to $200 more for their cars I could understand that they might close their doors and advise their customers of the increase. But that was not the situation. They were readjusting prices to meet the new duty arrangements, and it meant a lowering of cost to the consumer. No one can tell me that a firm who had so much business as obliged them to move their output daily from their plant would find it necessary to deprive their employees of two or three days' work in order that they might revise their prices. No, Mr. Speaker. It was merely a demonstration against the government in this country, and as such it was both unwise and unfair.

CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure that the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) will excuse me if I do not follow him through the specially assembled figures he has presented to the House-figures which will not convince any man in Canada without a job that the country is as prosperous as it should be when we consider its great natural resources. But my hon. friend gave some figures regarding the French treaty, and during the latter part of his remarks I took the trouble to check them. He pointed out that the government had done a great thing for the country by negotiating that treaty, and he gave certain figures of our trade with France before the war and after the war. I happen to have under my hand figures for the years during which this treaty has been in force. I find that in 1923 our imports from France were 812,204,000, and our exports $14,118,000; in 1924 our exports were $15,767,000, and our imports $18,887,000; 1925, imports $18,460,000, exports $10,290,000. In other words, during those treaty years-because half of 1923 was under this treaty-we have had a decrease in our exports to France of $3,828,000 and an increase of our imports from that country of $6,255,000. To put the matter in another way, before this treaty came into effect we had a favourable balance of trade with France of $1,913,000, whereas in the last fiscal year that has been converted into an unfavourable balance amounting to $8,170,000. This, I might say, would apply in almost equal degree to our treaty with Italy, and I believe also to the other treaties which have been negotiated by this government.
The minister also went on to quote certain figures regarding the woollen industry, figures largely from the United States, and concerning one particular company in Canada. No amount of figures can explain away the fact that from 70 per cent to 75 per cent of our woollen mills many of which had been in existence for from forty to sixty years, are now closed owing to the uncertain or adverse actions of the present government during the past four years. The minister also recited certain alleged facts regarding the reduction in taxation last year. He was only quoting what the Minister of Finance said, and he stated that there would be a reduction of aproximately $20,000,000 in our taxation. I would like to point out to the House, Sir,
The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

that this reduction has not materialized. This year we have paid very much more in duties and a much larger amount in sales and other taxes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not in percentages, though.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The percentage was not changed; certain articles were only last year removed from the sales tax. The sales tax was changed during the previous year. I am not a pessimist, Mr. Speaker, I have always been an optimist and I believe the Conservative party of Canada are not pessimists. But I would point out that great credit is sought for this government on the ground that during the past year we had a period of prosperity in Canada. While I believe that, owing to acts of Providence, certain benefits have been received especially by our farming communities, we know that in the great majority of cases conditions to-day are no better than they were twelve or twenty-four months ago. We have simply struck a favourable tide for the time being, owing to certain circumstances over which this government has no control. It is very easy for a boat to drift with the wind, but if you drift with the wind only it will very often change and the boat will get nowhere. It is absolutely necessary to do something in order to reach the shore. In regard to our circumstances during the past year I might read the Speech from the Throne in that regard, which says:
I congratulate you on the growing prosperity of this favoured land. The products of our agricultural and other basic industries have greatly increased. Our export trade shows remarkable expansions. Our manufacturing and related .industries throughout the Dominion have experienced a development not enjoyed in many years.
I would like to ask the ministry, who put these words into the mouth of His Excellency, where they found the information to justify that statement. I am quite sure that in the part of Canada with which I am familiar hundreds of factories have closed; no new factories have been built, and thousands of men are to-day without proper employment. As I said before, there is a reason for our apparent prosperity. We have had a good crop year in most provinces, and we have enjoyed a period of great prosperity in our mining industry. This industry, fortunately, is not under the control of the Dominion government, but looks for its prosperity to the various provincial governments. Speaking for the province in which I live and which I represent to a greater or less degree, we have to thank the present provincial government

and Minister of Mines for the vast increase in capital which is to-day going into northern Ontario. I would also point out that a part of our prosperity is due to the greatly increasing tourist traffic in Canada. This tourist traffic within a few years, I believe, will be one of the greatest industries in Canada. We have at present millions of dollars invested in taking care of these tourists, and millions more are being invested every day. It is an occupation which requires neither tariff nor free trade; it simply exists, and I think the Acting Minister of Immigration (Mr. Stewart, Edmonton) would be well advised in doing a certain amount of advertising in order to assist this industry. If he would simply show the various points of interest to those who desire to come to Canada he would be doing a good work. Many of these men who come from other countries become permanent residents of Canada, and in the meantime they invest a large amount of money in this country.
I was going to show that the proposition of the government regarding the prosperity of Canada was not altogether in accordance with the facts. I have in my hand a copy of the Public Accounts, and I see that during each of the years from 1920 to 1925 there has been a decrease in the note circulation of this country. That, I think, is a fair indication of the prosperity of the people. The total of our one dollar and two dollar bills in circulation in 1920 was $29,789,653; to-day it i3 $27,911,606.50, a decrease of over $2,000,000, or 8 per cent. In the total circulation of Dominion notes we find that there was $311,932,791.92 in 1920 and $206,712,088.46 in the last fiscal year, a decrease of $105,000,000, or 34 per cent. If we take the notes issued by the various chartered banks, we find that in 1920 the total circulation amounted to $225,769,628, while to-day it amounts to $157,888,900, showing a decrease of $68,000,000, or 30 per cent. These decreases are most interesting, because they give a real picture of the circumstances of our people.
I might also point out that our commercial failures are not decreasing. I have in my hand an extract from the Ottawa Citizen of Saturday last, giving the commercial failures in Canada for the previous week, as reported t>y R. G. Dun & Company:
During the past week failures totalled fifty-five, in comparison with twenty-one in the corresponding week a year ago.
This is the condition under which the government claims prosperity.
A fourth industry which has been prosperous is our paper industry, which has been going

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
ahead by leaps and bounds in spite of any action the government may have taken. This is one of the principal reasons for such prosperity as we have. I would also point out that in our cities, regardless of their situation, there is very little building as compared with that of a few years ago. We find thousands of houses left in the hands of the builders, for which they can secure no purchasers. If we contrast that condition with the state of affairs under which this government took office five years ago, a great difference will be seen. It was necessary for this parliament at that time to vote twenty or twenty-five million dollars for a housing scheme in an effort to keep abreast of the demand for houses. To-day the exact opposite is the fact with the exception of one or two cities in Canada, and I might point out that these are the very cities which have enjoyed apparent prosperity during the last two or three years, and they are the very ones which are being hit by the government in this budget.
The industrial population of Canada is very large, and they are to-day in a position which, to say the least, is not envious. They are working part time, hanging on under conditions which are very, very unsettled. They are waiting for one thing; they are waiting for some government to come into power which will give adequate protection to Canadian trade. I do not think there is in Canada to-day a city or town that has not had idle factories or idle men or men who are working part time. Thousands of factories have *closed, and many of them have failed during the regime of this government. I hold under my hand Hansard of last year, which shows that in a debate on April 14, 1925, the then Minister of Labour placed on Hansard certain figures which have been disputed from time to time, but, as I say, they were placed there by a then member of the government, and he points out that during the fiscal year of 1922 there were 857 manufacturing failures in Canada; in 1923, 792; and in 1924, 625. These were all manufacturing industries which had failed during those three years, and their liabilities were as follows: In 1922, $39,000,000; 1923, $31,000,000; 1924. $36,000,000. In other words, more than 2,200 manufacturing firms failed in business in Canada during the regime of the present government. Outside of the few exceptions that I have mentioned, namely, factories concerned with lumbering or the pulp industry, it is a fact that we have no new factories in Canada to-day, nor is there any encouragement in the present budget to induce capital to invest in this country.
But the most unsatisfactory feature of the whole situation is the uncertainty that pre-14011-181
vails throughout the country. It is not the action of the government so much as the threats which the government have from time to time made against the people of Canada. The government themselves apparently knew that, for they placed in the mouth of His Excellency in the Speech from the Throne words that would indicate that they desired to quell public unrest, and they assured the people of Canada that no tariff changes would be made without careful investigation. I know that these words have been placed on Hansard before, but in order to complete my remarks I shall read them again:
They-
That is, His Majesty's government.
-believe that in the interest of industrial development every effort should be made to eliminate the element of uncertainty with respect to tariff changes; that changes in the tariff should be made only after the fullest examination of their bearing upon both primary and manufacturing industries and that representations requesting increase or decrease of duties should be made the subject of the most careful investigation and report by a body possessing the necessary qualifications to advise tk** Ministry with respect thereto.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this country is in a perfectly healthy state, ordinarily speaking. We have great natural resources, and we have public spirited men who are perfectly willing to go on and develop these resources under proper conditions, but the principal drawback is the fact that we have to-day a government which has condemned itself. The Prime Minister has stated that this government is, and has been, in no condition to make any forward movement in Canada. Take his own words at Richmond Hill. Speaking of the government's continuing in office, he said that if continued in power:
At the most we would be reduced to marking time. This is not a moment in our country's affairs at which to mark time. It is a time to march forward.
Further on, dealing with the majority which he then had, or did not have, in parliament, he said:
I would say further, I do not believe that any one of the four can be dealt with effectively by a government which is not supported by a substantial majority in the House of Commons. Group government and minority government may be inevitable in transitional phases of our political history, but neither is the kind of government wherewith to achieve great reforms.
I was going to say this government reminds me of a stoiy I heard many years ago of a young lady who made up her mind that she was averse to marrying certain kinds of men. In the first place, she said she would not marry a red-headed man under any condition. Nor would she marry a cripple or any man who was deformed. She

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

would not marry a widower, and she certainly would not marry an old man. But as the days went on, she decided to strike the red-headed man off her list of ineligibles, and decided that she would accept him, if necessary. After a while, as there were so many crippled men after the war, she decided that a slight disability would not make any difference. Time went on, and she decided that perhaps a widower, if he was a young man, would be all right. But he did not come along, and then she decided that she would take practically any man that came along, and she finally married an old, red-headed widower, with six children and a wooden leg. That has been practically the fate of this government. The right hon. leader of this government said that he could not and would not continue in office under certain conditions which at that time were certainly more favourable than the conditions under which he is attempting to govern at the present time. He further said that certain reforms could not be made without a sufficient majority, that without such a majority no important legislation could be put through the House, and yet to-day he is trying to make the people believe that he is giving them something like good when he has no majority at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, and it has a brake, but the brake might slip too, and then they would go down faster than ever.
Now, I desire to say a few words regarding the budget itself. The country will undoubtedly welcome the decrease in the income tax, a decrease which should have been made at least two years ago in exactly the same degree. Even according to the statement of the preceding speaker, the hon. Minister of Public Works, it would have been far better for this government to have reduced the income tax as they pretend to be doing than to have made a fake change in the tariff two years ago, and it -would have been better for business in every way. The United States have decreased their income tax twice since it was first instituted. It was never as high as the tax in Canada. I do not know that I need go into the figures; they have been placed on Hansard, I think,
TMr. Arthurs.]
before, but I will cite a few of them. The rate for married men earning $3,000 in United States, under the act of 1924, was $7.50. In Canada it was $40 and it remained at this figure until the present budget. On a $4,000 income in the United States the tax in 1921 was $60, and in 1924 $22.50, but at present it it is only $5.63. The Canadian rate during all this time has been $80. And so I might go on, all down the list. It is easy to prove to any reasonable man that a reduction in this income tax has long been due in Canada. We find that in Great Britain there have been two reductions in income tax amounting on the whole to upwards of thirty-three per cent. Australia has reduced her direct taxation, and I believe another reduction is due. Up to 1925 the tax had been reduced from $19.44 per head to $11.32 per head, a reduction of $8.12 per head of population. If we applied these figures to the population of Canada it would represent a reduction of approximately $70,000,000 to our people, and this reduction, as I said before, would have assisted in keeping capital in Canada and aiding business throughout the country. New Zealand has also reduced her taxation twice, and the reduction is far greater in amount, than that now proposed by the Canadian government. I repeat that had this reduction taken place long ago, as it did in other countries, we might have retained more working capital in Canada.
The same arguments would apply to the-reduction in the postal charges, with this addition: We found that when penny postage was first inaugurated in this country instead, of the government losing money by the change they made money; the receipts of the Post Office Department were greater after the reduction than they were before. Personally I have no doubt that approximately the same result will follow the present reduction.
The tax on receipts was mentioned by the Minister of Public Works. I do not know that I need to go into details on the question. To begin with it was a stillborn child of this government. Nobody ever had any use for the tax, and the government simply took off one that was put on by themselves.
Now, let me deal for a few moments with, the matter of the sales tax. As has been pointed out, the sales tax, previous to this government coming into power, was approximately three per cent-rather less in some cases. In 1922 the government raised the tax to four and a half per cent, and in 1923 they raised it to six per cent. In 1924, experiencing a great change of heart, they brought the tax down to five per cent and then claimed a.

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
reduction in taxation; but whereas the tax was three per cent under the Conservative government the present rate is five per cent. The collections under this tax amounted to $66,707,390 in 1924-25, or $7.50 for every man, woman and child in Canada. The collection for the last fiscal year, that is to say 1925-26, amounted to $71,900,000, or $8 per capita. This only includes the amount received by the government, and those of us who are business men know that before this tax reaches the ultimate consumer it is increased fifty per cent over that figure as a profit on the amount paid for the tax. The people of Canada are labouring under a very severe burden in respect of this sales tax. The government are getting after everything. I find in my own constituency that where a poor settler, starting to make a home for himself on a bush farm, cuts a few logs and takes them to a mill to make lumber in order to build a house, he is charged the sales tax upon the sawing of that lumber. It would be just as reasonable to charge a sales tax upon the threshing of wheat or the milling of grain for a farmer's own use. However, this is the condition as we find it to-day, and I hope the Minister of Finance will look into the matter fully when he comes to read Hansard, and provide an adequate remedy.
There is one good thing about the sales tax, though. This time the government have seen fit to reduce it upon certain specified articles, and we learn that we are to have the tax entirely removed upon pot barley, pearl barley and split peas. Surely the government does not think that soup is going to become absolutely necessary for the welfare of the people of this country. Yet these three items named in the resolution are the only three upon which the sales tax has been removed.
Before leaving the subject of taxation I wish to say a few words as to the statements made by the Minister of Finance regarding taxation, and the new divisions which he has made-that, is to say, the taxation for war purposes and the receipts derived from war revenue. I have no very great exception to take to the classification he makes, but I should like to point out that he has charged as a war expenditure the difference between the amount of interest upon the public debt as of 1914 and the amount as at the present time. It is quite apparent to anyone who thinks of the matter for a moment that in any event the debt would be larger in 1926 than it would be in 1914. It will also be apparent to anyone who knows the conditions and the amount of advances to our railways that the debt would 14011-181J
be considerably more than it was in 1914. Taking the ordinary average increase for the preceding ten or twelve years-I have taken a ten-year period-not allowing for special conditions and advances and loans to railways, I find that a most unfair charge of $6,575,000 has been made against war expenditure. We find that payments in connection with the Soldier Settlement Board have been so charged. I might point out that the great business of this board at the present time is building up farms for incoming settlers from foreign countries, principally from Great Britain of course-farms that have been thrown up by the soldier occupants, and they are expending upon them large sums of money in order to put them in better condition for intended settlers. Certainly there is no reason why that money should be charged against war expenditure. When we have regard to the amount of the public debt-because after all that is the primary and greatest charge against our income-I point out that the government have given no attention to special receipts arising out of the war. They have received from Great Britain over $60,000,000 in adjustment of war expenditure. They have also received large sums from Belgium, France, Greece and Roumania. But there is no corresponding credit given, and if those matters were properly adjusted we would find we were receiving more under the so-called war taxes than we have expended or are expending.
I come now to the tax proposals of the government. In the first place, only one of the tariff proposals made, is attracting attention in the country to-day; I refer to the reduction in the duty on automobiles. I have no brief for the automobile industry. There are no automobile factories in my county or in its vicinity, nor I believe are any accessories sold there. But I would point out to the government that we do not know whether or not the automobile manufacturer or the manufacturer of the accessories has been taking excessive advantage of the tariff in the past. The duty on these things had been the same for many years past until this budget was introduced. We all know, as was pointed out by the Minister of Public Works a few minutes ago, that there was an attempt last year in the form of a resolution introduced in this House, to lower the duty on automobiles. That resolution was voted down, and I note that every member of the government who was present at that time voted against it. Ten hon. members who were then or are now ministers of the crown were here when that question came up, and the speech made by the Minister of
The Budget-Mr. Arthurs

Public Works (Mr. King) was directly opposed to any reduction of the duty. Furthermore, there is a duty just as high or higher upon many other articles which are at least as necessary as automobiles. If the government have decided that low priced cars are a necessity or that they are an implement of production, why not remove the excise and sales tax?

because the excise tax is purely and simply a luxury tax. We have also been told that the sales tax should be removed from every article of production. If that were done, the reduction by the amount of the sales tax and the excise tax would mean that the price of a .5 p.m. car would be cut far more than it will be reduced under the provisions of the present budget, and in the meantime the position of these factories, and the employment of those thousands of men and their fellow workers whom we saw in Ottawa a few days ago, would not have been jeopardized.
I do not know anything about the automobile industry. I do not know whether they have been taking advantage of the 35 per cent duty accorded them in the past, and I am quite frank in saying that I do not believe any member of the government knows more than I do about the matter. They have no means of knowing, yet they are going ahead-for what purpose I do not know, although I rather suspect it. The government argue that the automobile manufacturers have made too much money under the 35 per cent tariff If that is so, why not give the House a list of the companies, a memorandum of their earnings or of their profits and losses?-because there has been loss in many cases. Let them give us the amount of business done by each company and the income tax collected from each. This would be a simple matter and would show that the government know something about it. I am quite safe in saying that the Minister of Finance has not such a statement under his hand, and that he, like the others, is simply going blindly forward. If we had a statement of that kind; if government officials are competent and honest-and I have no reason to believe they are not- it would show the true state of the automobile manufacturing industry in Canada, and the same would apply to the accessories.
In the meantime all we are asking the government to do is simply to fulfil the direct pledge which was given that there would be no change in the tariff without strict investigation. I have already presented that pledge to the House in another connection. We as a party, or I personally at least, only ask
{Mr. Arthurs.]
the government to stay their hand until the investigation which they themselves have promised-a procedure which at least is fair and honest-has been made. Every member of the then government or of the present government who was here last year voted against the motion for a similar reduction or a reduction of any kind. Why this sudden change? Why this utter disregard of the loss of employment and other injury which may result to industry? There is only one answer. The first reason is that they need the vote of the western members, who were the instigators of the movement in the first instance. In the second place we have today Conservative members representing those centres, which are most vitally interested, whereas a year ago the members representing those constituencies were Liberals. In the third place there is a certain section of this House, I believe-and I am saying that in no invidious sense-which is willing to support anything which will punish Ontario. They do not expect to carry Ontario at the coming election and they are prepared to let that province go to the wall so long as it does not hurt their own interests.
The other night an hon. member read at great length a speech delivered by Henry Ford'. I do not know that that has anything to do with the matter. If I were in Henry Ford's place I would do exactly what he is trying to do. I would advocate the same doctrines he is advocating to-day, the same doctrines Mr. Carnegie advocated after he had got the United States Steel Trust in the position in which he placed it. He was quite willing then to be a free trader, and so is Henry Ford when he has practically a monopoly of the market in automobiles. We are not asking the support of men of that kind. We as a party are asking that we should have a tariff that will build up our trade, or that will do the very things in a greater or less degree along the lines which have made Mr. Ford and others a success. We want to build up our own factories and keep our own people here, not drive them away. The Minister of Public Works said something about the exodus from Canada-it is just matters like this which are driving our young men to the United States. I gave the figures last year with reference to the emigration of native born Canadians to the United States, showing that in the preceding three years 540,000 young people had left this country for the other side. I think the hon. member for Huron at that time showed from the same source that in the ten years preceding some. 700,000 Canadians had gone to the United States. That may be true, but the period

	The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
included years when some Canadians went to the United States for a purpose that did not reflect any credit on themselves. But during the same years mentioned by that gentleman 265,000 men returned to Canada, according to the certificate of the United States government, or an average of 26,500 per annum, whereas during the last five years there have returned an average of less than 2,500 per annum. Our Canadian officials may of course give figures different from these, but it must be remembered that they take into account men, women and children who are returning to Canada temporarily to spend a month or two in the summer. I know that as a matter of fact for some of my own relations have been so treated in the statistics: they have been entered as returning to Canada although they are permanently resident in the United States. We should take our figures from one authority, and the statistics given in the annual report of the Commissioner General of Immigration of the United States I would commend to the House. Hon. gentlemen can get the book in the library and if they will look up the figures they will find that they are indeed alarming. Now I come to another branch of the tariff as it affects the farmers of Canada. A large ' percentage of Canadians who have been looking forward to some relief from the budget have been disappointed. These people do not ask a reduction but, on the contrary, an increase in the tariff in order to protect themselves. Since this government came into power four and a half years ago great changes have taken place in tariff matters throughout the world. Every country of which I have any knowledge has increased its tariff in that time, and this is particularly true of our friends to the south. The one in particular I want to discuss now is the Fordney tariff, in which a very material increase was made in the duties on farm products entering the United States. The United States duty on such products is in some cases many times higher than our own, while others are absolutely prohibitive. I shall not put these figures on Hansard, seeing that they were very ably discussed yesterday by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuar-rie). Besides, they are familiar to hon. members. Strong representations have been made to the government that the Canadian agriculturist, the mixed farmer at least, should be accorded a fair tariff which will preserve the home market in view of the fact that he is debarred from the United States. Many of our Progressive friends sneer at the idea of a home market; they claim that their	product depends entirely upon the foreign market. The prices for the things they produce, whether wheat or anything else, are controlled altogether by conditions abroad, and therefore they see no benefit in the home market. It seems to me that many of the arguments they advance and some of the figures they quote must have been prepared by someone who either had not made a close study of the subject or had had a brainstorm. The member for Maple Creek (Mr. Spence) made certain statements, as will be found at page 2680 of Hansard of April 21, 1926. He said: In my own province of Saskatchewan we have, roughly, $500,000,000 coming in from our wheat crop alone, and aibout three-quarters of s. billion, in round figures, for all field crops. We have one billion and & half dollars corning into Canada as a whole from all agricultural products. Then to show his appreciation of the industrial element of Canada he says: We have three million people engaged in agriculture. I am sometimes inclined to smile a little when I hear my hon. friends talking about industry and its importance. They speak of some shoe factory employing a few hundred men, or some automobile manufacturer employing a few thousand men, and turning out a few hundred thousand dollars' worth of automobiles. This shows how carefully some gentlemen consider the conditions in Canada. Speaking from his own point of view the hon. gentleman declared that our dairy industry alone was worth more than the products of all the mines and all the oil and gas wells in Canada. Had he taken the trouble to look up the statistics he would have discovered how wide of the mark he was in many respects. The statement that we receive in Canada one: and a half billions from agricultural products strikes me as absurd on the face of it, and I do not believe anyone who has looked into the matter believes that. I have here a return giving, article by article, the exports from Canada of agricultural products during the past calendar year, and showing where they went, whether to Great Britain, to the United States or elsewhere. A few of these things give evidence of the adverse effect of the Fordney tariff on the farmer of Canada. We exported last year $5,990,000 worth of apples, of which only $150,000 worth went to the United States. Of barley we exported $24,000,000 worth, the United States taking only $10,000. Our exports of oats amounted to $23,000,000 and of this sum the United States took only one-quarter of one million dollars worth. One of the few exceptions to this long list of adverse trade relations with the United States in these commodities is wheat, of which the United States took from

The Budget-Mr. Arthurs
us $12,219,000 worth. This commodity did not pay the forty-two cents American duty, and that is why it went into the United States. They imported this wheat to raise the grade of their own flour so that it might successfully compete against the Canadian miller in Canada. In other words, they imported this wheat entirely in the interests of the American manufacturer.

Of wheat flour we exported $74,000,000 worth, sending only $67,000 worth to the United States-not one dollar in one hundred thousand. The same thing is seen in cereals. The second table relates to animal husbandry, and the figures are under the same headings-raw, partly manufactured and fully manufactured. I pointed out that the hon. member for Maple Creek was a long way wrong when he said we received a billion and a half dollars for the products of the farm. Mr. Speaker, I think I

We have a ibiHiion and a half dollars coming into Canada as a whole from all agricultural! products.

my hon. friend from South Huron to try to lead me to think I made a mistake. with smuggling; the hon. gentleman may know. I would also point out other items which are peculiar so far as farm products are concerned. I am using these figures principally to show that some of the statements made by our friends to the left are, to say the least, wide of the mark.
The assertion was made the other night- 1 think by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar)-that our exports to Australia last year were $105,000,000. Although that figure was repeated twice by the hon. gentleman, I felt satisfied there must be something wrong. On looking up the exports to Australia I find that in 1924 we sent to that country goods to the value of $19,000,000- not $105,000,000. In 1925 that value dropped to $12,000,000-under the Australian treaty. So the hon. gentleman was overstating the exact amount by almost ten times!
I have already remarked, Mr. Speaker, that sometimes the arguments advanced by our friends to the left are not exactly fair to those of us in this part of the House, nor are they exactly fair to the eastern provinces. We find the impression is sought to be conveyed by certain hon. gentlemen that the eastern provinces, especially Ontario and Quebec, are endeavouring for their own profit to take everything they possibly can out of the western provinces. This has been the stock argument of our Liberal friends in the western provinces for some time. I do not think it -would do any harm to point out that this is not always the case. I have before me the official figures for last year and the year before of the various federal duties and taxes collected, and I am quite within the mark when I say that the provinces of

Ontario and Quebec together have for years paid over eighty per cent of our total federal taxation; that next comes British Columbia; and that during the last two years at least there has been collected from the three prairie provinces only eight per cent of the total Dominion taxation.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
wide of the mark. In order to show the benefit the farmer has received I will quote an eminent authority. If the hon. member thinks the farmers are receiving no benefit from the Crowsnest pass agreement, I would refer him to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) for information. I have in my hand a Canadian Press despatch of a speech made by the hon. member for Brandon a.t Elkhorn just previous to the last election, in which he is reported to have said that had there been no Progressives at Ottawa there would have been no Crowsnest pass rates. He is also reported to have said that these rates were worth $20,000,000 a year to the central western provinces. There can be no doubt of that authority.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that I will detain the House longer. Most of these subjects will come up at another time and I shall be pleased to discuss them when they are again before the House. In closing I might point out that there is nothing in this budget which will help the people of Canada.

There is no relief for the farmers, who are suffering by reason of an adverse tariff; there is nothing giving an extra day's work to our factories; there is nothing to induce new factories to come to Canada and nothing to induce the re-opening of those factories which are idle; there is nothing to indicate a policy designed to have our raw materials further manufactured in Canada for the benefit of Canadians-simply the same old course as that pursued by this government during the past four years. The idea of this government is to hang on to power, and to drift. It may be easier than pulling against the stream, but I want to point out to hon. gentlemen opposite that you will never get any higher if you are content to drift down with the current.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed the address to which we have just listened from the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs): It was a moderate speech, and although I do not agree with his deductions, 1 believe he was entirely sincere, as indeed I believe all hon. members are in fhe speeches they make in this House. I shall not enter into any of his arguments at the present time, but shall touch on certain points as I go along.
I want to join, first of all, in the chorus of congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and the government on the budget brought down. The many tributes that have been paid to the government from different quarters of the House and by all sections of the country are, I believe, well justified. The budget itself is in plain phraseology. Everything is shown in clear detail. There is no camouflage; there are no hidden mysteries. It lays bare the facts in a way that all may read and understand. The plain facts are good enough; they do not need to be coloured or concealed. The Finance minister's presentation was couched in good, clear Anglo-Saxon, from a people's government to the people themselves. In its genuine) modesty it reflects its author. I believe the budget will appeal to the people in all walks of life in this country. The Finance minister did not find it necessary to make comparisons between this period and other periods or between this government and previous governments, for as someone has said, it is a budget that speaks for itself.
As I listened to the different speakers, a saying of Lord (Macaulay came to my mind. That is the best government, he said, which desires to make the people happy and knows how to make them happy. It was Bright or

The Budget-Mr. Tobin (Wetaskiwin)
Cobden who said that a government whose legislation does not give relief to every humble cottager in the land has not solved the problem of government. These sayings come back to my mind as I read the budget and couple it with the Speech from the Throne; for the two together make up a programme that I believe will bring relief to all the people of this land.
I do not intend to go to any very great length or to any very great depth in dealing with matters to which reference may be made in the debate on the budget. I think of the first speech Mrs. Nellie McClung, delivered in the Alberta legislature, of which she is still a member. She tried to show her position as a new member and to state her idea of how she should speak as such. She compared her position with that of a curler. When the curlers go on the ice, she said, they slide down a number of rocks to get the run of the ice, and I am going to get the run of the ice, she said, before I venture very far afield. I have made up my mind, Mr. Speaker, that I do not want to venture too far in this House before I get the run of the ice, and I would like to suggest in the most friendly way to some of the new members opposite that if they would first get the run of the ice they would probably do better in the long run, and there would not be so many speeches made that the authors would afterwards like to have deleted from the records.
Coming to the budget itself, I find that the expenditures for the year have been kept belorv the estimated figures and that the estimated revenues have been exceeded. The national debt has been reduced, and the National railway has progressed beyond our fondest hopes. It is to-day reaching to the goal where it will require no more funds from the national treasury. That is made plain in the budget, and the showing of the railway alone wTould be a credit to and an achievement for any government in this Dominion.
The people are going to be asked to dip into their pockets for $25,000,000 less of taxation this year than last. Now that may seem a small amount to some people, but I think it shows the trend of affairs when taxation is being reduced to the extent of $25,000,000.
The return to penny postage will simplify things very much. Three will not divide exactly into five, ten, twenty-five, fifty or a hundred, and when I go to the post office to buy stamps I always have to figure how many stamps I should get for a certain sum and how much change I ought to have.
