You can figure that more easily. I am glad to see that the receipt tax has been done away with. I have received a great many letters from my constituency expressing the hope that this tax would be abolished. You can put your stamp on a cheque, and if you have not the necessary stamp you can make the cheque out for two cents extra. But in the case of the receipt stamp, somebody may want to pay you money he owes when you are on the train or out in the woods, where no stamp is available. You naturally want to get the money, and I am glad that the government has seen fit to remove this tax.
I am sure that the reduction in the duty on automobiles meets with the approval of all the western provinces, and I think of the eastern provinces as well. I have read the newspapers on both sides of politics, including the Edmonton Journal, the Calgary Herald and the Vancouver Province, and all seem to agree that the right thing has been done. The people want automobiles, and want to get them as cheaply as they can. There is one phase of this question that I should like to put before the House. I think the difference in the price of the same make of automobile here and in the United States has had a bad effect on' immigration. People will compare the price of an automobile here with the price of the same car in the United States, and finding a big spread between the two they naturaly conclude that if there is this difference between the price of automobiles in the two countries, the same difference applies in other lines of goods. They cannot make such a comparison in the case of other articles, hats, for * instance, or clothing, because they may not be the same kind of article. But the Ford or the Dodge car is the same here as it is in the United States, and people notice the large spread in price between the two countries. That, I think, has done a lot of harm.
The same is true of the income tax. People can figure out exadtly what they have to pay in this country and what they would have to pay in the United States. We are still paying a higher income tax than they are across the line, but we are now approaching equality, and I am glad that this is so. The income tax as changed affects particularly the man with a small salary. The man who enjoys a salary of $3,000 used to pay $40 income tax; to-day he pays nothing. A man in receipt of an income of $3,500 formerly paid $60; to-day he pays only $10. The man
2858	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Tobin (Wetaskiwin)
with a salary of 14,000 formerly paid $80; to-day his tax amounts to only $20. I think this is a move in the right direction.
Now, the splendid achievements of the past fiscal year and the promising outlook for the coming year are not the results of chance or accident. Shakespeare has said that men are sometimes masters of their fate. He might just as well have said that governments are sometimes the masters of their fate. These achievements have been brought about because the present government when they assumed office in 1921 took hold of the administration of public affairs with the determination, as the ordinary man says, "to make it go." The gratifying improvement that has come about is due to the business ability of the present government and their bullheaded determination Ito win. When they (took office in 1921 they had faith in themselves, in Canada and in the Canadian people. I unhesitatingly affirm that no government that ever assumed office in Canada was faced by such difficulties and handicaps as those which confronted the King government in 1921. The previous administration, if we are to judge by the admissions made by some of its members, had apparently lost hope in themselves and hope in the country. In what other light are we to read the last budget speech of Sir Thomas White in which he expressed himself as follows:
The world Is sadly out of tune. Trust and confidence is sadly lacking. Class interests are advanced with t sellish insistence. Unemployment is with us. Faith in our fellow men is weakened. Doubt of the future is voiced, and what is the trouble0 The sun still shines, the rivers still sparkle and our lands are as fruitful as ever; our resources just as great.
Having painted the desolate picture that he did, the then Minister of Finance exhorted parliament to remember that the sun was still shining and the fields were still fruitful, and Providence in this case was asked5 to come to the assistance of a Conservative government. Well, Providence did come to their assistance and relieved them of office and put the present government in power. To-day the opposition say that everything good that has happened in the country is due to a kind Providence. If that be true, when hon. gentlemen opposite had) a heavier burden than they could carry it was Providence who relieved them of that burden and placed it on the shoulders of the present government.
I have already said that the present government replaced an administration which seemed to have fallen into a state of despair. The country suffered from an adverse trade balance. During the last two years of the last government the national debt was increased by $174,000,000. It kept piling up at a tre-

mendous rate, and the cost of government kept pace with it. The adverse trade balance was most marked during the years 1911, 1912, and 1913, amounting in the aggregate to $736,000,000, perhaps the greatest adverse trade balance in the history of the country. And in the years which followed, agriculture fell into a deplorable condition, business was depressed, the Canadian dollar fell below par-* and the value of the dollar reflects the financial status of a country; upon it outside financiers and other countries base their opinion of the credit and the solvency of a country. Not only was the Canadian dollar at a considerable discount at that time, but Canadian securities and bonds were falling in value, and the people were greatly disheartened and discouraged. The national debt rose to $2,422,000,000.

In 1921. My hon. friend seems to dispute that. Well, that is according to my best information. The King government assumed 'office under all these handicaps: an enormous adverse trade balance, the cost of government increasing, and the national debt mounting at a tremendous rate. When the Liberal party were in power previously the national debt amounted to only $350,000,000, but when they once more assumed the administration of public affairs in 1921 it had advanced to $2,400,000,000, in round figures. Under those conditions it was a herculean proposition for them to attempt to carry on the government of the country. It took men of vision and courage to grapple with the situation. The task could only have been undertaken by men animated by a grim determination to bring back order out of a state almost of chaos.
How was the task accomplished? The new government, as the saying is, put their house in order. First of all they devoted their attention to effecting retrenchment in the governmental expenditure. I believe that in the budget speech of last year it was shown that the cost of government had been reduced by twenty-five per cent. The ratio of governmental expenditure then stood as three to four; that is to say, the new government spent only $3 to every $4 which had been spent by the previous administration. Then a reduction was brought about in the tariff in order to encourage the basic industries. Hon. gentlemen will remember the great reduction which took place in the duty on farm implements in 1924, and the prediction made by the opposition at the time that the

The Budget-Mr. Tobin (Wetaskiwin)
concerns engaged in that industry would go out of business, and that Canada would be ruined. The results have been just the reverse. To-day the Massey-Harris Company, the Cockshutt Company and the different other concerns engaged in that business, are doing well.
The next matter to which the government gave their attention was the expansion of trade by the arrangement of commercial treaties with other countries. A great deal has been done in that direction, and more will be done in the future along the same lines. In future if we go to the West Indies we shall be able to see the product of our flour mills, our smoked hams and bacon, our biscuits, our hay feed and other products, being unloaded at different ports in those islands. When the present government came into power they realized that the home market was not at all sufficient for a great producing country like the Dominion of Canada.

speechtext:
(Wetaskiwin):	When the
House rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to show the conditions that obtained in Canada when the present government took office in 1921. I had referred to the trade of the country, the growing cost of government, the
outlook for the agriculturist, the depression in business, the falling value of the Canadian dollar and of Canadian securities and bonds, the distressed condition of the Canadian people, and the immensity of the national debt. I was then going to show what methods the government had taken to restore order and prosperity in Canada, and in this connection I mentioned governmental retrenchment, reductions in tariff duties and the extension of trade by means of commercial treaties. One other subject of vast importance to Canada remains to be dealt with, namely, the problem of transportation.
In reference to automobiles I should like with the permission of the House to put on record in Hansard a statement which, although it has already appeared, is of such moment as to warrant repetition. Henry Ford, as we all know, is one of the best recognized businessmen on the American continent. Not only has he made a colossal success of his business in the United States, but -he owns a large proportion of the stock of the Canadian Ford Company. The article in question has a very important bearing on the present situation, and without reading it I will ask to have it published in Hansard. It was an interview by Mr. Ford in which he confirmed a. previous interview and added to it. He said:
As a manufacturer of automobiles in Canada he believes the tariff to be a hindrance and stupidity.
Mr. Ford surprised people with something of this opinion in a brief remark after visiting his great Canadian plant on Wednesday. This afternoon he enlarged on the subject, confirmed his statement that free trade would benefit industry, gave his reasons and explained their application to the manufacture of Ford cars in Canada.
From the conversation came voluntary statements of pertinence and encouragement to Canadians, that it is possible to manufacture as cheaply in Canada as in the United States, that Ford cars in Canada have been selling at a higher price than necessary because of the tariff, that the tariff encourages industrial indolence and tends to permit prices based on what the market will pay rather than on proper costs of production, that the Ford Company of Canada, and presumably other Canadian companies will develop greater efficiency and economy of manufacture as a result of the proposed tariff reductions. Would he offer an opinion which might be useful to Canadians who are perplexed?
"You people are just waking up," said Mr. Ford in reply. "You ought to rub the other eye now, too, and clean out the tariff."
"Would it be a good thing for your company in Canada?"
"Certainly."
"The tariff is a hindrance to trade. I would have free trade. I believe in free trade everywhere."
"Do you mean by that that you can manufacture a Ford car as cheaply in Canada as you can here?"
"I can. Give me that plant at Ford City and I'll compete with the plant here at Highland Park any day. Why shouldn't I? Our unit in Canada can buy as cheaply as we can here. We make every part of the car in the Canadian plant and ninety-five per cent,
2860	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Tobin (Wetaskiwin)
over eighty-five anyway, of the raw material is supplied right in Canada. We get our steel from Algoma, lumber, everything we need."
"The usual answer," I suggested, "would be that large scale production makes the difference. Many Canadian manufacturers believe that they cannot compete with American manufacturers because the latter have advantages in mass production."
"I don't see that," said Mr. Ford, "What do you mean by mass production? I think we've got large scale production in our Canadian unit. They're turning out six hundred cars a day."
"How many are you making here?"
"Oh, we're doing between seven and eight thousand a day, but I don't think that's any advantage after a certain point."
"Do you mean that large scale production ceases to be an advantage when it grows beyond a certain degree?"
"Yes," said Mr. Ford, and explained that costs of manufacturing are almost equally divided between labour and raw materials. In both of these items, he argued, the Ford Company of Canada is as favourably situated as the American plants.
"In fact," he added, "you have a better class of workman in Canada than we have here, more intelligent, more vigorous. I like to look at their faces. They're mostly Anglo-Saxon."
"If it is true then," I said, "that the Ford car can be made as cheaply in Canada as here, why have we had to pay a much higher price for it all this time?" "The old story," replied Mr. Ford, with a twist of his shoulders, "Because they have been able to get the price, that's all."
"Because the tariff has made the higher price possible?"
"Yes, certainly they've been able to get a higher price in Canada, naturally they've taken it."
"It is quite evident that the consumer will benefit from tariff reduction by lower prices," I said, "but you say that the automobile manufacturer will benefit also. Can you explain in what way?"
"Why, yes," replied Mr. Ford in some surprise, "It's quite simple. Lower prices mean more buyers, more buyers mean more business, more business means growth for the manufacturer. I would cut out the tariff," he repeated, "and have free trade. Free competition brings healthy business. I can tell you that those fellows over in our Canadian unit are going to manufacture more efficiently now. They'll have to it's going to be a better plant over there, better organization. That's another reason why it's a good thing for the manufacturer."
"You believe then," I asked, "that to help the manufacturer one must first help the consumer, and if the consumer benefits the manufacturer is bound to benefit?"
"I don't know any other way," replied Mr. Ford briefly.
"Some people," I explained, "believe in the reverse process. They say that tariff reduction will kill manufacturing in Canada, that there will be unemployment, and no wages, and therefore no money for the consumer to spend, that you must first help the manufacturer in order to help the consumer."
"That's all wrong," said Mr. Ford.
In the matter of transportation the present government, we are all pleased to know, has placed the Canadian National railway system on a strictly business basis. This system was in bad shape in 1921 and the government, having looked the globe over for a man with a sufficient knowledge of the transportation business, at length discovered one-large in 
avoirdupois, large in business ability, and large in optimism. The result the Canadian people know. To-day the Canadian National railway system is not only one of the best transportation concerns in Canada and in the North American continent, but it has been so equipped and built up as to measure up in efficiency with and offer real competition to the best transportation system in the world, the Canadian Pacific Railway. The efforts of the government in this and other reforms have led to the following conditions: Wte have a favourable trade balance of over $400,000,0010, a balance which is steadily increasing, while business in all commercial and financial circles to-day is recognized as sound. You have only to read the financial newspapers, the reports of banks and insurance companies and of commercial enterprises generally, to confirm this statement. Business in the country is on a sound basis and is increasing. These results have been achieved since the present government came into power. Now we have a balanced and more than balanced budget, accompanied by a reduction in the cost of living as well as in the cost of government. Furthermore, our dollar has its full purchasing power, so that financial institutions in this and other countries look upon the solvency of Canada to-day in a different light as compared with the condition of 1921. Our National railway system is a pronounced success, as I said a moment ago, and our bonds are buoyant, being sought after by all buyers of securities. The present state of affairs shows, therefore, a very marked improvement over the period preceding 1921. In this phenomenal improvement our good friends opposite-and I am sincere when I refer to them in this way- can only see and believe that the hand of Providence has been partial to the Liberal party. If that is so, I would advise the government to continue to work hand in hand with Providence.
The condition of affairs as shown by the budget will stand out in all the greater relief by reason of the fact that so many have been giving us such dismal pictures of the country during a number of years past. We have heard " the whisper of death," and blue ruin has been preached with wearisome persistence. We all remember the election campaign of October last. You will remember the blue ruin stories that were circulated throughout the country. What will the people who heard those stories, and in a measure believed them, think now? Then in the debate on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne the House will remember some of the blue ruin speeches with which members

The Budget-Mr. Tobin (Wetaskiwin)
of the opposition favoured us. I hope I will get the ear of the government for the suggestion I am now going to offer them. I think it is the duty of the government to see that every elector be sent a copy of this budget together with some excerpts from the speeches of our lion, friends opposite condemning all things in this country and prophesying national disaster. In my opinion the electorate are entitled to this information so they may contrast the prosperous condition of the Dominion to-day with the gloomy forebodings of our friends opposite during the years they have been in opposition.

In Alberta we had an opposition party. But that opposition was too strenuous and worked itself out of business. speechtext:
Thank you. I want to read the opinion of a well-known Canadian journalist on the prospects of the Pacific trade. Mr. John Nelson, speaking in Toronto on November 12 last, said:
"Treat the Pacific as our forefathers treated the Atlantic. Be Drakes and Frobishers, explorers undismayed by foreign lands and foreign tongues, so you willl create a new Elizabethan age and grow rich with the art and culture no less than the economic wealth of Cathay."
This was the advice which John Nelson, well-known Canadian journalist, left with the members of the Empire Club when he addressed them ait luncheon to-day on the problems of the Pacific as .they affect Canada. The address was based on observations he had made this summer in Honolulu at a conference of the Institute of Pacific Relations, a gathering of 120 delegates representing nine countries.
Canada's orientation in foreign affairs should be "oocidentation," said Mr. Nelson. The Occident was calling to Canadian statesmen as well as to Canadian merchants, and the future of the country was on the [DOT] Pacific even more than on the Atlantic.
"Premier Mackenzie King," said Mr. Nelson, "has declared that our prosperity is bound up with our export trade. Where will we find greater opportunities for new markets than in Japan and China."
He was impressed by Canadian ignorance of the Pacific which eqnalled the whole land area of the Globe. Canadians knew the Mediterranean. It was the cradle of their culture. They knew the Atlantic, it had been the main highway of their commerce, but they were still unaware of the importance of the Pacific. Even the United States was unaware of it until the Spanish war, .the acquisition of Pacific .territory and the foresight of Roosevelt, had drawn attention to the fact that Asia meant more than Europe to the future of this continent.
I read Mr. Nelson's opinion merely to show you what great possibilities there are for Canada in connection with trade over the Pacific. This year Canada exported 14,000,000 bushels of wheat to the Orient. Two years ago there was no export to that part of the world, and the western provinces were in a bad position with regard to the shipment of wheat. We found that other countries had to ship only a distance of 400 or 500 miles to the seaboard, but we had to take it across the continent. To-day we find as China and Japan are learning to use wheat the western provinces of this country are going to be in an enviable position-one of the best positions-in regard to the shipment of wheat, because they will be able to ship a large part of it straight across the ocean to the Orient. So that things are changed in western Canada, I hope for the good and welfare of all the Dominion.
The hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Arthurs) this afternoon advocated a tariff for the farmers. I hope that the agriculturists of this country will never fall for such a proposition, because it would be the undoing not only of the farmer but of the whole country. The United States might just as well say that it is the greatest free trade country in the world, as the hon. member says it is the greatest high tariff country. You find the coal fields in one part of the United States, the cotton belt in another part, the sugar cane and fruit in another district and the iron in another. The states are almost self-contained; they trade among themselves. We are not so situated. We have no cotton, sugar or oranges. The experiment which they are trying in the United States is proving expensive for the farmers. The farmers may be slow to learn, but they will learn that that policy is against their interests, and I hope the agriculturists of this country will never listen to protectionist arguments. I admit that the right hon. leader of the opposition, by his power of debate and his great ability, may make some inroads among the people with his line of argument; there is no doubt about that. But we must gain our experience from that of the United States, and it is a good thing for this country that their policy is going



The Budget-Mr. Tobin (Wetaskimn)
to fail before there is a possibility of its being adopted in Canada. That fact will save us if nothing else will.
The prosperity and success of all interests in the east, both commercial and financial, depend first upon the western crop, second upon transportation and markets, and third upon the price paid for the various manufactured goods received in exchange for those products. Those who do not understand the position should come out west and see the needs of that country. The pioneer farmer of the west, will start probably with an axe, -not much more-later on he will have a walking plough, then a riding plough and eventually he may reach the stage of gasoline power. His demands are never complete. If you allow the farmers of the west to become prosperous, I can assure hon. members listening to me to-night that there need be no fear of the rest of the Dominion, because they must trade; they are great buyers. They have put all their profits, up to the present at least, into some other commodity. If the west produces hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of products the people there do not deposit that money in the bank; they spend it and will continue to spend it for many years to come. Upon the prosperity of western Canada, therefore, largely depends the prosperity of all the other parts of Canada.
The enacting of the legislation promised in the Speech from the Throne means encouragement and inspiration to all parts of Canada. Some of this legislation has reached the stage where there can be little doubt that it will be passed by this House, and I desire briefly to refer to it. I mention first the revaluation of soldier settler lands. In the district I represent there are many soldier settlers and they have wanted this legislation for a number of years. Some of them have left the land, but others have carried on manfully and are doing well under the difficulties of their present position. They will not expect every detail to be made right at once; it cannot be done. I think the attitude of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), who presented the bill for the soldier settlers, must be looked upon favourably by hon. members of this House in that he tried to make changes suggested by the opposition and showed a desire to make the measure conform with the wishes of all parties, as he himself stated in this House. He wanted to satisfy all the people in the country by this soldier settler bill. I cannot see that the bill has been improved very much by the changes, but the minister has shown the right disposition. I am glad that there is to be a

revaluation of the soldier settler land. I was pleased that during the debate no one took any position adverse to the measure; nobody said to the opposition, "This is all your doing, the trouble was caused by you." I am sure the soldier settlers will be glad to see this bill become law.
The old age pension bill is the highest type of legislation and will be welcomed by all fairminded people. It is our moral duty to see that it becomes law.
Then we have the amendment to the Penitentiaries Act, under which all inmates of penitentiaries are to be allowed to do useful work, apart of the proceeds of that work, I understand, to go to the dependents of the inmate, if he has any; otherwise to be kept in trust for himself. This move by the government is a wise one. When inmates of a penitentiary are permitted to do useful work which agrees with them mentally, work that they know something about, they will not have time to reflect on their misdoings; they will not feel that the world is trying to take vengeance on them, and in many cases they will become reformed. There is some good in all people, and this reform will mean much. It is humanitarian and it is right. I am glad that this matter has been brought before the House, and the hon. member (Miss Macphail) deserves to be congratulated on her move in this direction.
I wish to make a few brief references to my own province and to conditions prevailing there. I suppose I need not tell the House that at the present time there is 9 p.m. an oil boom in Alberta. While we do not want unreasonable booms, I believe there are good prospects of finding petroleum in that province in large paying quantities, and I suggest to the government that they should take a part in helping to bring about a realization of our hopes in this respect. Every year large tolls are paid by Alberta to the Dominion in permit fees. In order to give you an idea of the amount of those fees I will place them on record:	The total fees for the last current
year were $454,911. In April last it was $2,944; in May $6,000 odd; in June $1,000. and for March this year the figure stood at $64,000.
I would suggest to the government that they do one of two things: either give bonuses for the production of oil, say for one or more producing wells in the north of the province and one or more in the south, or themselves drill wells in these sections. There is always a suspicion, when strangers drill for pil, that the intention is not to market the product
28*7

The Budget-Mr. Tobin (Wetaskiwinj
immediately but to hold it for speculative purposes. In my opinion the government could stimulate oil production in Alberta and it would mean a good deal to the Dominion at large. We firmly believe that there is oil in the province and I hope that the minister will act on the suggestion I have made.
As regards the cattle situation in Alberta, there is some complaint on the ground of duplication of fees. The cattle market is not very attractive to-day, as the prices are low and the farmer has altogether too many tolls to pay to get any profit out of the business. In the first place he must of course meet transportation charges, and besides this he has to pay feed and auction bills. He complains that at the first town into which he takes his cattle he must pay a veterinary surgeon to examine the stock, and if he ships them through to Winnipeg they must be examined a second time at Calgary or Edmonton. Very frequently there is only one veterinary to be found especially in a small town, a good deal of trouble being entailed hunting him up. Then there is the condemnation insurance, as I believe it is termed. When the farmer sells his cattle at the stockyard he pays fifty cents per $100 by way of insurance, the argument being that though the animals may be in good condition at the time of sale they may afterwards be found to be diseased. I do not see why the farmer should be expected to comply with a condition of this kind which does not obtain in any other business. When you buy an article from a merchant he does not give you a fee by way of guarantee that you will find nothing wrong with your purchase when you have taken it home. In my opinion this condemnation insurance should be abandoned. The people do not know whether the government is running the thing or whether the stockyards are in control of it. I understand that the entire fee is used for administrative purposes, but this notwithstanding, I contend that it should not be charged at all. It may be said, I know, that if the fee were not paid the farmer would possibly receive a lower price for his cattle, but I do not think that this contention is sound. At all events it is an unwarrantable impost.
I come now to a subject which is of considerable importance to the province of Alberta, namely, fox farming. In Alberta the people are finding it necessary to engage in other things besides the growing of wheat. They are going in for gardening and they have made a success of the raising of bush fruits. It has been demonstrated at the experi-H011-182f
mental stations in the province that such things as currants, gooseberries and raspberries may be grown in Alberta just as well as anywhere else. The people are learning too, to beautify their homes horticulturally and in many other ways. In the raising of foxes they have an industry that holds out considerable promise for the future, but there is one anomaly to which I would call the attention of the government. When the fox farmers of Alberta want an inspector to examine their foundation stock they are obliged in most cases to send to Prince Edward Island, which is a considerable distance away. That is one of their chief complaints. It may be of interest to the House to know how many inspectors there are in the fox industry throughout the Dominion. The inspectors, who I may bbserve in passing are obliged to put in a week's special training in Ottawa, are allocated to the provinces respectively as follows: British Columbia one, Saskatchewan one, Manitoba, one, Ontario, four; Quebec, one; New Brunswick, four; Nova Scotia, one; and Prince Edward Island, thirteen. It will be observed that Alberta has not even one. This may seem a trivial matter, but when it is remembered that an inspector has to come, as is usually the case, all the way from Prince Edward Island to examine foxes in Alberta it will be seen that an injustice is done that province. Last year about 1,310 foxes were examined in the province. The fox ranchers are therefore anxious to have inspectors located right on the ground. I may mention that the fox that brought the most money in Canada in any year was one that had been raised in Alberta. The value of foxes raised in the province last year for breeding purposes and pelts amounted to something like $6,000,000. The bulk of the product went to the United States, although a good deal of it is shipped to Europe. I understand that the fox industry yields the largest revenue of any in Prince Edward Island.
Another matter of importance I want to refer to before concluding. We have in the province of Alberta some beautiful lakes, many of them being attractive resorts with hundreds of cottages all around. I might mention Gull lake for instance. I think the Dominion government might very well supply suitable fish for propagation in these lakes, so as to produce fish, as well as provide good sport at these points. Pigeon, Conjuring and Gull lakes in my district are particularly interesting and something should certainly be done in this regard to improve them as resorts and to make them attractive to fishermen.

ization of freight rates the transportation companies put on what they call a "permit" system, under which a farmer could not ship his grain westward unless he had bottoms at the coast to take his grain. Therefore, the grain dealers bought his grain at the Fort William price and naturally where it is to their advantage, they get the lower freight rate and any premium at Vancouver. That has taken place again this year. There was a partial reason for it in that a large amount of our grain was damp. I hope I can get the eye of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), for I know he will take an interest in this matter and back me up. I want his support.

Let me give some further particulars of Alberta. The province has an area of 161,872,000 acres. Of this, 97,123,000 acres represents arable land, and we have under cultivation 29,293,053 acres, leaving unoccupied arable land of an acreage of 67,829,947. In a word, we have the greatest acreage of unoccupied arable land of any province, and we are proud to think that this will some day be brought under cultivation and benefit the whole Dominion. Recently our local paper in Wetaskiwin reprinted an article from the Toronto Globe, entitled, "A Province to be Envied," and I will read it for the benefit of hon. members:
With the transfer from Dominion authority to Alberta of the natural resources of that province, the country will observe with particu.hr interest the progress made in development. Alberta coal has already made a reputation, but probably few people realize that it represents 14 per cent of the estimated coal reserves of the world, 72 per cent, of those of the British Empire and that Alberta cool mines represent an investment of more than $50,000,COO. Something is known of the existence of petroleum fields, and interest is re-awakened by recent publication of a report made by Dr. Hume of the geological suivey. When it is considered that besides the coal deposits, 80,000 square miles of the province have petrcleun. possibilities, and that, besides, Alberta leads the Dominion in the production of natural gas, it is evident that the wealth of this young province passes far beyond the sphere of agriculture.
Even the most ambitious province shouild be satisfied with 72,000,000 acres of land capable of agricultural development, an area large enough t. contain the population of the British Isles, but with varied and rich natural resources it has within itself the potentialities of a cosmopolitan nation. Behind the prairies, it is estimated, are 60,000 square miles of merchantable timber. For scores of miles along the Athabasca river are bituminous sands suitable for paving the streets of future cities. Extensive shade and clay deposits lie in the southeast. It has building stone, salt and bentonite. Its fisheries are worth hundreds of thousands of dollars per year. And what may be beneath the surface in addition +o the known resources may offer almost untold possibilities foi development.
An inland empire of such vastness, yet with a population of only 600,000, Alberta is in an enviable position to make its imprint dominant on the future map of Canada.	*

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Tobin) informed us that the farmers of the west wanted windmills. I can at least appreciate the fact that there was a considerable reduction in the visible supply of those articles in Wetaskiwin when the hon. gentleman came to Ottawa. That, with the addition of the gas which he says exists in that province and which has no doubt permeated his system, will probably account for the length of his remarks and the variety of the subjects which he touched upon. I noted one remark of his in which he credited the government with bulldog determination. The bulldog has never been recognized as an animal remarkable for its intelligence, but it has always been credited with a disposition to hang on; consequently I suppose that is the reason for the reference. The hon. gentleman quoted Cobden as saying that a government fails which does not give relief to the humble. I suppose he had in mind the relief afforded by this government to the thousands of people who have left Canada to find work in the United States.
The hon. gentleman also referred to Mr. Henry Ford, and was evidently quite willing to accept Mr. Ford as an authority on the automobile question. I am not willing to accept Mr. Henry Ford as an authority on anything, even an automobile. The machine which bears his name is said to be an automobile; it is also said to be several other things, the names of which I need not enumerate this evening. So far as Henry Ford and his industry are concerned I might point out that he is in a different position from that of any other manufacturer in the world. He has a largely capitalized industry with a perfected organization; he has mass production, and I daresay he would be quite pleased to have free trade with all the world so far as automobiles are concerned. But Henry Ford is a man who has shown that he recognizes protection. I believe that in September 1915 he bought fifty acres of land in Ontario with the declared intention of building a tractor plant which was to employ 10,000 men. The government saw fit to remove the duty on tractors, with the result that Henry still has the land but the plant has not 'been erected. Henry Ford would never have established a factory in Canada if it had not been for protection. He thought he would supply the French trade from his factory in England, but France put a heavy duty on automobiles and Henry was obliged to put up a plant in France. He also built a plant in Ireland1, I believe, and in several other countries. When Mr. Ford

Mr. Ford is a man who has made a great success of life from the financial standpoint; he is among the wealthiest, if not the wealthiest, man in the world. But he has some peculiar ideas. I believe he launched at one time what was called a peace ship; then he had an idea for a "synthetic cow." Asked what his idea was, he said he was going to do away entirely with the four-legged animal. "Where are you going to get milk?" he was asked, to which he replied, "I am going to manufacture milk chemically to supply the public. There is no further need for cows." Henry's synthetic cow was going to solve the problem. So I say when we speak of Henry Ford and quote him, it is well to remember that we are quoting a man who, while he has made a great success of the particular business which carries his name, is recognized as possessing some very strange peculiarities.
The hon. gentleman made several references to other things. I am not a sufficiently well-trained mental acrobat to follow him in all his various peregrinations and wanderings, and I shall not attempt to do so. He referred to one or two things also mentioned by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) to which I wish to give just a little attention.
The hon. gentleman and the Minister of Finance made reference to the national debt of Canada, and I would also like to say a word or two on that subject. In 1896 the national debt of this country was roughly $258,000,000. In 1011, when the Liberals went out of office, in round figures it amounted to $340,000,000; in other words, they had added $82,000,000 to that debt in fifteen years. Between 1911 and 1014 the debt was reduced by $6,700,000. Then the war came on with its tremendous costs, and by 1921 our debt was in round figures $2,350,000,000.- In 1925, according to the statements given by the Finance minister recently, it was $2,417,437,685 and on March 31 of this year amounted to $2,395,000,000. In connection with the national debt I wish to quote a statement made by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), who in 1921 was Finance minister. In presenting his budget that year he said:
If we deduct the bare cost of the war but charge up pensions, soldiers' civil reestablishment and interest on the war part of our debt, none of which we would have had but for the war, our debt to-day would be $115,000,000 less than in March 1914."
He also made this statement, which was never contradicted, which was accepted as a fact and is a fact:	The revenues for the

last year, he said, exceed the ordinary expenses of the country, including all pensions and all current war charges, by $69,400,000. I wish to add another statement made by him on that occasion. War obligations have been met, he said, and paid to the extent of $698,809,700. I quote that statement, Mr. Speaker, because I want to apply it to the debt of this country. I want people to understand what that debt means and how much of that debt was due to the war.
During the years 1917 to 1920 inclusive we put through in this House seventeen appropriation bills totalling $1,755,705,235. No amendment was moved to any of those bills, nor was a motion made to strike out one single dollar of those appropriations.
I wish to call attention also to how seme of this money was spent. We paid out in soldiers' gratuities, $164,000,000. May I add that that was a matter of expenditure dealt with by the Conservative government, and which was done with and settled and had not to be considered by this government after it took office. We also paid out $102,000,000 for soldiers' civil re-establishment; $90,000.000 for pensions; $80,000,000 for soldier land settlement; $7,000,000 for soldier insurance; $25,000,000 of a housing loan; $10,000,000 for technical education; a special grant to aid agriculture of $10,000,000; another grant for roads of $20,000,000; and our shipbuilding cost us some $30,000,000. The items I have enumerated total $538,000,000, and I want to emphasize this fact, that not one single dollar of that amount was challenged by any member of the House.
I want also to emphasize this fact, that many of the items to which I have referred, and which bore very heavily cn the exchequer of the country at that time, the present government has not been required to deal with because they were dealt with and settled before they came into office, so they were relieved of that burden.
I would also like to add that in the last three years of the Conservative regime, in 1919, 1920 and 1921, we collected in total receipts during those years a little over $1,098,000,000. In the next three years, 1922. 1923 and 1924, this government collected $1,191,000,000; that is to say, the present government, or the government in power after 1921, had in the first three years they were in office $100,000,000 more revenue to run the country with than their predecessors had in the last three years they were iD power.

The budget, Mr. Speaker, is always a matter of great public interest, especially to those whose large investments may be sacrificed and those whose daily bread may be jeopardized by the stroke of a pen. There has been a good deal of misrepresentation of the Conservative party in regard to the tariff. I wish therefore for a few minutes to discuss the subject, going back a little way in history.
Between 1878 and 1896 we had a protective tariff in Canada known as the National Policy. Having regard to the threats made by the 'Liberal party for eighteen years while
out of office there was a good deal of apprehension as to what they would do on coming into power. The Laurier government came into office in 1896 and the people found that Liberals in office were a different sort of people from Liberals out of office. At all events, fortunately for the country, that party maintained the policy and principle of protection throughout the fifteen years they were in power. There is absolutely not the shadow of a doubt about that. They went out of office in 1911. The issue in that election was the reciprocity pact, but even in proposing reciprocity the Liberal party did not depart from the principle of protection in relation to manufacturers. Between 1911 and 1921 the Conservative and Union governments still maintained the principle and policy of protection, and that principle and policy may be said to have been carried out by the present government, fairly well at least, up to the session of 1923, when the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding presented his last budget to parliament. In that year, in delivering his budget, the Hon. Mr. Fielding said:
There is a thought which does not receive as much consideration as I think sometimes it should be given in public discussions, and that is the desirability of somethin" like tariff stability. Business men do not like to be always threatened with changes in the
tariff....The tariff as it will be when the changes
proposed to-day come into effect will be a moderate tariff and probably as low as the country can afford to have under present conditions. Of course we cannot expect that it will be satisfactory to everybody. It will not meet the desires of those who would rigidly apply the principles of free trade. It will not meet the wish of the advocates of high protection.
The leader of the opposition at this point interjected:
It comes pretty close to it.
Mr. Fielding went on:
I think the country should be content to accept the tariff as it will now stand as one as fair and reasonable as can be prepared under all the circumstances, and business men should be able to carry on the various enterprises without the fear of being soon disturbed by further changes.
That was an announcement on the part of a man who for some seventeen or eighteen years had occupied the position of finance minister of the Dominion, and however much any of us may have differed from him politically, I think I am putting it correctly when I say that the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding was respected from one end of Canada to the other by those of his own political party and also by those who were opposed to him politically. I think I am also correct in stating that it was because he and Sir Lomer Gouin were then members of the government that the wreckers, represented by the hon. member

Whereas the tariff policy of the government, as indicated by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, and particularly his pronouncement in favour of tariff stability at existing rates, and the consequent intimation that the government contemplates no further appreciable tariff reduction, constitutes a repudiation of the tariff planks in the Liberal platform of 1919 and is inconsistent with the Finance Minister's statement last' session that the changes then made were a step in the right direction.
So we see in these words of the hon. member for Brandon that stability of tariffs is something to which he apparently objects. He said further:
And whereas the fiscal policy of the government as now brought down is based on the principle of protection, and in this respect is indistinguishable from that of their predecessors in office.
I quote this because it bears out my statement made a moment ago that during the whole time of the Laurier government's tenure of office and down to 1923 the principles of the national policy as laid down by the Conservatives were adhered to by the Liberals. There is another reference here which will bear reading in the light of the attitude now taken by the hon. member for Brandon in regard to the Speech from the Throne. He said:
Therefore, be it resoflved:	That while recognizing
that changes in the fiscal policy should be made in such a way as to give industries affected a reasonable opportunity for readjustment, this House is of the opinion that the principle of protection as a basis for fiscal policy in Canada is unsound, and that every claim for protection should be heard publicly before a special committee of parliament.
So at that time the hon. gentleman apparently thought that industries affected should have a reasonable opportunity for adjustment. Has any such opportunity been given to the automobile industry? The hon. gentleman in his resolution also stated his belief that where an industry is affected it should be heard publicly before a special committee of parliament. Well, we have now the Tariff Advisory Board. I should like to know from the government if they have lost faith so soon in this board of their own creation. If they still have faith in it, why did they not carry out the pledge given in the Speech from the Throne, that all industries would have an opportunity of placing their case before this 
board, and that on the facts thus adduced parliament would act? Mr. Speaker, I make this statement that since the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne was passed, this House stands committed to carrying it into effect. Those who voted for it certainly, and the members of the government more especially, were pledged by the adoption of that Speech from the Throne-which they framed and placed in the mouth of His Excellency-to carry it into effect; and I do not believe, Sir, that in the history of this or any other democratic country on the face of the globe there has ever been such a flagrant violation of solemn pledges given before the election and reiterated in the Speech from the Throne as this government has been guilty of in connection with the adjustment of duties brought down by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech. I say that every member, especially on that side of the House, as well as every member who sits to my left, is in honour pledged to vote against that part of the budget, because if he does not do so he is repudiating the vote that he gave in support of the Address, and is therefore violating his honour as a public man.
A word or two more, Mr. Speaker, in regard to protection. We have had free trade theorists and free trade faddists in the country and in this House. I suppose we always will have them here until the people put the matter right by leaving them at home. The late President McKinley said on one occasion, "Nothing is cheap which enforces idleness on our people." I should like that statement to sink into the minds of every member, especially of those who profess to follow free trade doctrine. "Nothing is cheap which enforces idleness on our people." And idleness has been enforced on our people by the attitude and course of this government to such an extent that hundreds of thousands of our young men have been forced to go across the line to seek employment. The free trade theorists base their conclusions on two cardinal errors: first, that the burden of an import duty must fall upon the consumer; second, that a tariff must increase the cost of the article taxed. Both assumptions have been proved by experience and history to be absolutely false. The free trade theorist has a pet conundrum which he frequently brings forward when he seeks to annihilate his opponent: how can you cheapen an article by taxing it? I wonder if any hon. gentleman will carry his free trade ideas far enough to endorse that statement.
There are two distinct classes of import duties: Those levied on articles which are

The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Frontenac)
not and cannot be produced in Canada, for example, tea, coffee and cocoa; and those levied on articles which are or can be produced in Canada. In the first class the entire supply is imported and there is no possibility _ of competition between the dutiable article and the article produced here. In such case3 the duty is added to the price, subject however to such modifications as may be brought about 'by the use of substitutes. In the second ciass there are both inside and outside sources of supply. That produced at home is duty free; that imported bears a duty, and the duty on the imported article has the effect of encouraging the increased production of the duty free article supplied at home. I answer the conundrum, therefore, in this way: The article cannot be cheapened by taxing the whole available supply, but is inevitably made dearer. It is perfectly possible, however, and history and experience have proved it to be true, that taxing a part of the supply as is done by a protective tariff may cheapen the article by encouraging increased production of that part which is duty free because produced at home.
Let me illustrate that contention by some indisputable facts. In 1883 the duty on agricultural implements was raised to 35 per cent. Between 1886 and 1890 we had_ nineteen factories in Ontario alone making binders, as against nine factories in the same line of business in the United States. Did binders go up in price? On the contrary, the competition in Ontario was so keen that many of the firms went out of business because of the low price of the article they were selling. I heard it argued in this House by the Hon. Mr. Crerar, on one occasion, that the duty imposed obliged the consumer to pay the amount of that duty extra, not only on the imported article but on similar articles made in this country. Supposing, for instance, there was a duty of S10 on an American mower coming into Canada. It was argued that the man in Canada who bought an American mower would have to pay $10 more because of the duty; but it was also argued that he would have to pay $10 more on a mower produced in Canada because of the duty. I wonder if any hon. gentleman in this House will endorse that argument. It has been presented here before, and I say it is absolutely fallacious. Canada produced some 280,000,000 pounds of butter last year, 95 per cent of which is consumed at home.

My statement was and is that the duty upon an article produced to some extent in this country is shared; a part of it may be paid by the consumer here and a part will be paid by the country from which the article comes. There the law of supply and demand will govern.
Why, Sir, if it is argued that the duty adds so much to the price of the article, on the 280,000,000 pounds of butter produced in this country, with a tariff of 4 cents, the farmers obtain every year $11,200,000 more for their butter than they otherwise would receive. If you can make me believe that I will immediately advocate the raising of our duty on butter to 8 cents and then to 12 cents, so that the farmers will have $22,000,000 and $33,000,000 more to put in their pockets. If the imposition of a duty adds the amount of that duty to the cost of the article, our farmers are reaping an extra profit of some $7,000,000 on cheese; of some $6,000,000 or $7,000,000 on eggs because of the 3 cent duty imposed on eggs. They will also reap a benefit of some millions of dollars because of the duty imposed on oats, wheat, barley and so forth. No hon. gentleman in this House believes for one moment, I am sure, that the addition of the duty on all these article adds so much to the price. It is just as consitent and reasonable to argue that the price of butter, eggs, meat and so on is increased to the full amount of the duty, as to claim that a binder, a mower or any other implement has its price added to by the amount of the duty on that article One proposition is just as sensible and reasonable as the other, but neither is reasonable.
When the McKenna duties came into operation in October 1915 they placed a 33^ per cent duty on motor cars, motorcycles, pianos and other musical instruments, clocks and watches, and cinema films. What was the result? The price of foreign cars in England dropped 21 per cent; the price of British cars dropped 30 per cent and the number of men employed in that industry increased from 50,000 to 300,000. Let me give you another illustration. Free trade England passed what is called the Dyestuffs Import Regulation Act in 1920, under Premier Lloyd George. In June 1921 the price of dyestuffs was 4s. 4d. per pound. In December of that year, under the protective tariff, the price was 3s. 6d. per pound; one year later it was 2s. 6d.; in 1923 it was Is. a -pound, or a reduction in three

May I add a further statement? A committee was appointed by the United States Senate to inquire into the effect on prices of the McKinley tariff. That committee reported that in the first twenty-eight months of the operation of the McKinley tariff the retail prices of 214 articles of common consumption had fallen by 64 per cent, while wages had risen by 75 per cent. As a protectionist, Mr. Speaker, I claim that the duty is not added to the price except when people are entirely dependent on foreign supply. Primarily it is labour that is most interested in protection. The man with money can seek other avenues of profit or wait for his dividends, but the labourer cannot wait for his dinner.
There are a few things which I want to call to the attention especially of hon. gentlemen from the west. I want to refer for a few minutes to six staple articles of food-bread, butter, milk, meats, potatoes and eggs. Of these articles Canada as a whole produced an exportable surplus amounting in 1924 to 8384.000.000. Each province, however, does not produce enough of all these articles for its own use, and to the extent to which any province falls short of producing these necessities of life, that province affords the best market in the world for the sister provinces which have a surplus of those articles.
Let me refer for a moment to wheat, because it seems to me-perhaps I am unjust in this;
I do not want to be-that hon. members from the west make everything revolve around wheat. I know it is a very important article, very important indeed to the west, and I can understand to a certain extent their attitude,

but let me point this out to them: Canada exports wheat to some thirty countries. Canada exports flour to some seventy-nine countries. Our exports of wheat and flour, that is, flour converted into bushels of wheat, amounted in 1924 to 309.340,000 bushels. Let us look at our principal markets for that. First of all, our principal market is the United Kingdom, which in 1924 bought from Canada 173,000,000 bushels of wheat and 4,234,000 barrels of flour. Who was our second best customer? The United States bought from us, in 1924, 21,228,000 bushels of wheat and 221,641 barrels of flour. Taking wheat and flour together, perhaps some would say that the United States is our second best- customer, but so far as flour is concerned it is fourteenth on the list of Canada's customers. Our second best customer for Canadian wheat (is not the United States, but the Dominion of Canada, which in the year I have mentioned, 1924, required for food and seed some 85,000,000 bushels of wheat. Prince Edward Island had a small surplus; Ontario had a surplus in that year of over 7,000,000 bushels; Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and British Columbia ran short of their .requirements for food to the extent of 16,669,000 bushels, and to that extent those four provinces provided a market, that is for food purposes alone, to say nothing of seed, for the wheat of the west to the amount, of 16,669.000 bushels. They sent to the west over $20,000,000 to pay for that wheat, an amount just equal to the total received from the United1 States for our wheat, an amount double that received from Germany for our flour, an amount greater than the total received by Canada for our flour from our next fifteen be6t customers.
In this connection I might also mention that our exports of flour in 1924 represented 403,307 tons of by-products, which are of immense value to our farmers in the west is well as to those in the east.
It has been said that the price of wheat is fixed in the United Kingdom. Taken as a general statement, I think that that is true, but I believe it is subject to some modification. The average price of wheat for all Canada in 1924 was $1.22; in Manitoba, $1.24; Saskatchewan, $1.21; Alberta, $1.20; Ontario, $1.27. Each of these provinces bad an exportable surplus, comparatively small in the case of Ontario, but very, very large in the west. Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick had a shortage. In Quebec the average price for the whole year was $1.66; New Brunswick, $1.78? Nova Scotia, $1.61; Prince Edward Island, $1.59. speechtext:

mean in the case of butter?

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext:

provinces of Saskatchewan, Manitoba ,and Alberta had a surplus of about 27,000,000 pounds of butter.

speechtext: Then where does the selfishness come in? '

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are other provinces besides those I have just mentioned. My general statement was that
in cases where the prairie provinces required products, for instance British Columbia apples, they should buy British Columbia apples as readily as that province buys their wheat. That is the statement I make and, it seems to me, it is plain and easily understood. In regard to cheese, the prairie provinces did fall short. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta each fell short, the total shortage for the three provinces being about three and a half million pounds.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where did they get their supplies?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I cannot
say where they got their supplies. I presume they got them from the provinces which had a surplus. My argument is that is what they should do. Other provinces take your wheat, as in the case of the- provinces I mentioned a while ago. Seeing that the prairie provinces are able to market their surplus wheat in the province of Quebec and other provinces, then when those provinces fall short in their supply of cheese they ought to be willing to back up the industry which makes cheese in eastern Canada. But apparently that is not what they are willing to do. We in the east ask for and think we are entitled to a fair degree of protection in those articles which we handle especially.

speechtext: To make his argument fair the hon. gentleman ought to show that we are getting protection on our wheat such as British Columbia is asking for its apples. My hon. friend's argument is not fair unless he pomts that out.

speechtext:
I want to ask
the hon. gentleman

that a farmer in Canada, I do not care what he is producing, should, by a fair and reasonable adjustment of the tariff, be practically guaranteed that the article he produces will be used on Canadian tables instead of imported articles. be protected?

Still you go on raising more wheat. But what has that to do with my argument? I was arguing the point as to whether you require protection for your wheat or not. We will let it go at that as far as wheat is concerned and I will finish my argument with respect to the things that do need protection.

speechtext: Do you consider it fair to compel the producers in other parts of Canada to buy your articles at an artificial price when they have to sell their own products in the world's markets?

Now, Mr. Speaker, I have endeavoured to be as good humoured in this matter as possible, but my patience has about reached its limit. I do not propose to submit to any further interruptions of this sort from hon. gentlemen opposite. I have correctly estimated the intelligence of the hon. member for Melfort and have made allowance for it, but there is a limit beyond which even he may not be permitted to go, and I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to see that my right is respected and to prevent the hon. gentleman from acting as he has been doing.
Let me call the attention of the House to another point. They invested $100,000 in a subsidiary concern in New York known as the New York Export Company, and according to the sworn evidence of their manager their profits from that company in one year amounted to $530,000, or 530 per cent-this on the part ot heaven-sent politicians, the angels of political purity, who were howling their heads off about a duty of 12J per cent on binders. They objected to such a duty but they could take 530 per cent out of the farmers. Every vestige of profit this company made they secured from the grain they bought from the farmers, and from the implements and supplies they sold to them. Indeed, they made such exorbitant profits, as revealed in their own evidence given before a committee of this House, as would cause them to damn any company in the Dominion, outside their own concern, which had received even one-quarter of what they got. I say in the presence of these gentlemen, Mr. Speaker, that the most conscienceless, coldblooded, soulless profiteering monopoly that ever existed in the Dominion was the United Grain Growers' Grain Company, whose leaders framed the policy of the Progressive party that is now sitting in this House. I might refer to the profits they made on screenings. During those years, including the war, screenings averaged $8.84 a ton. When Mr. Crerar was Minister of Agriculture he bought some, as he said, for the benefit of

the farmers down east at $35 a ton. The government lost 896,446.46. He was Minister of Agriculture at that time as well as president of this big company in the west. In last 10 years United States has sold to Canada $2,000,000,000 more than Canada has sold to the United States.
This shows the effect which the Fordney-McCumber tariff had upon our export trade to the United States.
I want to say that that tariff was placed on the statute books of the United States at the demand of the farmers who live in the northern tier of states, where they have found it impossible to compete with the cheap farm production of the southern states. Half of the states in the Union, as their statistics show, report a reduction in the value of farms and in improved farm acreage. Where are they? They are in the northern part where their climate is similar to ours. The other half having a mild climate show an increase of farm acreage and farm values. The farmers of these northern states went to congress and said:	"We realize that we cannot
get protection against our neighbouring states, but we insist that we be protected against the importations from Canada and other countries; you can protect us to that extent." It was to meet that demand that the Fordney-McCumber tariff was passed. Those farmers just recently demanded an addition to the duty on butter, and at their request it was raised from eight to twelve cents a pound. In the face of these facts we are told that our farmers do not need any protection; we are
told that we are not affected by severe climatic conditions; when the dairymen of New Zealand and Australia are producing butter at the lowest cost of production, and our dairymen are producing it at the highest cost of production, we are told that we must not have protection. Hon. gentlemen like my friend from Rosetown (Mr. Evans) and some of those occupying the kindergarten from Saskatchewan repeat that they are not particularly affected, that the only thing they are interested in is wheat. Apparently they. do not care anything for the people of Ontario and Quebec-the two provinces which to-day are paying seventy cents of every dollar collected to run this country-the people of those provinces in the estimation of some hon. gentlemen in this House are deserving of no consideration at all. I realize quite well of course that the government and its assistants are actuated by a spirit of revenge. They do not like the result of the elections in October last; they will like even less the results when the next elections come around not only there but in other parts of the country.

speechtext:
The only
other matter I wish to refer to is immigration In the speech from the Throne it is said:
We have formulated and put into operation a comprehensive immigration plan.
What comprehensive plan have they put into operation? What comprehensive plan have they even formulated? Plans they have spoken of every year, one, two, three, but I should like any person to tell me of one single plan in regard to immigration which this government has put into successful operation Even their plan to bring out 3,000 families from Great Britain has fallen down. I am informed that the government notified the railways not to bring out any more families under that scheme. Why? Well, they say they cannot provide them with farms. -1 have some information in regard to that, Mr. Speaker. I have in this hand a list of over 700 farms in Ontario, prepared by the provincial government. Those farms are available. In this other hand I have a list of 656 farms in the little province of Prince Edward Island. Those also are available if the government choose to place settlers upon them. I have a further list of '55 farms in that province I have another list of a similar number of
2886	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Edwards (Frontenac)
farms in New Brunswick, farms running from as low as $150 up to $800 and upwards. Here is a 50 acre farm, 25 acres cleared, price $1,000. Here is a 232 acre farm, 150 acres cleared, house barn and good water, price $4,000. Here is a 50 acre farm, 25 acres cleared, good buildings, price $400. Here is another 50 acre farm, also 25 acres cleared, with good buildings, price only $700. Those farms are in Prince Edward Island. The New Brunswick list contains farms, with buildings and running water, priced from as low as $800. There are numberless opportunities to place the proper kind of settlers in the Dominion; they need not all be sent to the west. The places which need to be filled up are those older provinces of Ontario and especially the Maritimes. But the trouble with this government is that in immigration matters they are a ten cent government dealing with a hundred dollar matter; those are about the correct dimensions. The immigration question is the big question of to-day, and therefore it never can be successfully handled by the aggregation across the way. They have never handled anything of any size; they cannot do so, because they have not a capacity for anything big, and never will have. Anything done in immigration matters since this government came into power has been done by the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Railways, the different provinces and certain organizations such as the Salvation Army. Meanwhile our farmers are asking for farm help; no assistance is coming from this government because, as I said before, they are absolutely inadequate, inefficient and do not know how to deal with big questions.
It has been repeatedly stated that the Conservative party stands for a high protective wall, a brick for a brick. That is not true, Mr. Speaker, and never was true. I have shown that in the eighteen years from 1878 to 1896 we had a protective policy; that in the fifteen years of the Laurier government that protective policy was maintained; that the tariff on dutiable goods under the Laurier government was 5 per cent higher than the tariff on dutiable goods when the Conservative party went out of power in 1921. That apparently will not stop these hon. gentlemen from repeating what has already been said so often. Up until 1923, when the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding brought down his last budget, all the parties in Canada had fairly consistently followed the traditional National Policy laid down by the Conservative party in 1878. That policy was departed from when the King government lost the services of the only two [Mr. J. W. Edwards.!
of its members who had any standing in the country, Right Hon. W. S. Fielding and Sir Lomer Gouin. It then ceased to be a government, and there has been nothing since which could be dignified with the name of government. It has been getting worse and worse all the time. When we had those two big men in the government they could hold such wreckers as the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) in check, as well as those from Saskatchewan occupying the kindergarten seats. When these big men went out and the mantle fell on the pigmy shoulders of the present Minister of Finance and his colleagues, there was no one left to stem the tide. Since 1923 this has been a government of compromise, pussyfooting, log-rolling and bartering foi power; nothing else. They have thrown theii promises and pledges to the winds; they have violated the pledge given during the last election campaign, which was reiterated time and again. Where in this Dominion, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, will you find a man with money to invest who will show any confidence in this government? Who can have any confidence in a government which has violated its pledges, as this government has done? They have not only injured the automobile industry by their reductions regardless of their promises, but they have done worse; they have absolutely deprived the people of this country of that which is absolutely necessary, if you are to have industrial development-confidence in the government which controls affairs. They have destroyed that confidence, and by that action have struck a severe blow at the development of this Dominion.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, having taken so much time.

I can only leave the matter with them, hoping against hope that Providence, which has done so much for the Liberal
