subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with some hesitation that I rise to address this honourable House. If I do so it is because of a sense of duty which I feel towards this country, and in an especial manner to the county of Wright, which I have the honour to represent in the federal parliament.
So many able speakers have preceded me, representing the three-indeed I may say the four-parties of Canada in this House, that I felt my views might be construed by many as "a voice in the wilderness". I have not the gift of oratory; I am a simple business man, somewhat lacking in flights of eloquence, but content to possess at least the virtue of sincerity.
This is my maiden speech. Mr. Speaker, and I am sure some of the hoary statesmen who are listening to this my first utterance on the floor of this House, remembering their first efforts, will listen to my few remarks with sympathy and attention.
The budget as introduced by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) will not only receive my wholehearted support but commands as well my admiration for its eminently fair and just policy towards the different economic industries of our country. I do not claim it is perfect, but 1 do maintain that it is the best policy under existing circumstances in Canada. When we consider the terrible burdens, financial and otherwise, we have had to shoulder since the world war, I consider it a marvellous tribute indeed to the present government, that in spite of reduced taxation, they have succeeded in reducing the national debt by so many millions of dollars. Penny postage, whioh originated under a Liberal government, has been re-established by a Liberal government. The income tax has been materially reduced, and taxation in other matters has also been reduced. The consequence is that the farmer, the labourer and the man of modest means sees daylight and comparative prosperity ahead, while a few, and only a very few, moneyed interests 'are finding fault with a government that is honestly and intelligently doing its utmost to render justice and fair play to all, without favouritism to any particular class or privileged class. There are those who are criticizing the tax on the automobile industry, and declaring that it means the ruin of this important industry. A close analysis of the true facts of the case will not bear out their argument. The automobile industry is on a solid and thriving
basis. Let us only take last year's turnover and sales as an example. I quote from the Montreal Star of April 22, 1926:
The automobile industry attains record for 1925 output. One car to every 13 persons in Canada. Figures show record production was attained in the automobile industry in Canada in 1925, according to a statement just issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics at Ottawa. In that year, the eleven automobile factories in Canada produced 124,458 passenger cars, 22,144 trucks and 15,368 chassis, a total of 161,970 cars which was an increase of 22 per cent over 1924, and 10 per cent above the figures for 1923-the previous best year, when 147,202 cars and trucks were produced.
Does any intelligent member of this House imagine for one moment that the reduction in the tariff on motor cars is going to kill this industry? Far from it. As we say in French, my mother tongue, "c'est pour rire".
As regards the smuggling which it is said was going on, it is comforting and consoling to learn that there was an increase in the net sum collected in customs duties. There will always be a certain amount of smuggling in this country, as in all others, but our government is to be congratulated for the zeal and courage it is displaying in the prosecution of this investigation.
It has often been said of the Liberal party that it panders only to the agricultural interests, that it is at the beck and call of the farmer, especially those of the western provinces under the leadership of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke). If it were true-and I deny it-I would be glad to see our government favouring the agricultural classes of this country. In Canada they are to-day, and will be for many years to come, the predominant industry and the backbone, marrow and sinew of Canada. I have the honour of representing an essentially agricultural county, the county of Wright, in the province of Quebec. Our agriculturists are men and women of worth; they are the sturdy, healthy and progressive pioneers of our country-I use the term "progressive" advisedly. I will continue to support the present government in all its just measures for the welfare and advancement of the great Canadian west; and let no man forget that t)he prairie provinces were founded on 'toil, sacrifice and perseverance; and justice, if not humanity, calls for fair play to these worthy pioneers. As long, Mr. Speaker, as this government continues to protect the agricultural interests of this country, it will receive my wholehearted support. I must congratulate the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) in his effort to promote forestry conservation.
Lobster Fishing Season

It is a regrettable fact that $15,000,000 has been lost to us annually through criminal negligence and otherwise. I am glad to see that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. King) has interested himself in this subject. Outside of the prairie provinces, they have no direct legislation, but they have the force of advice, co-operation and co-ordination.
I am also in accord with the present administration in its old age pension policy. I would go even further and support a measure that would reduce the age at which the pension should begin from 70 to 65.
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, let me ask you and this honourable House: Is there to-day a more prosperous nation than Canada? Let us not be pessimistic but optimistic as regards the future of our country and Canada's wonderful natural resources. What Canada requires to-day is the spirit of optimism, not pessimism.
I am sorry that I have taken so much of your time, Mr. Speaker, and I thank the House for its generous attention.
On motion of Mr. Smith the debate was adjourned.
Mr. Lapointe moved the adjournment of the House.
I hope the leader of the House will not be offended if I ask for confirmation or denial of the late reports that certain changes in the budget are to be announced shortly.
